subtopic: REPORTED RESTRICTION ON LOANS ON HOUSING NEAR AIRPORTS

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert H. Winters (Minister of Public Works):
subtopic: REPORTED RESTRICTION ON LOANS ON HOUSING NEAR AIRPORTS
speechtext:
On Wednesday last, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Garland) asked a question regarding loans under the National Housing Act on property in the vicinity of airports. Subsequently on Thursday the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Fraser) asked the same question. This problem has been under study for some time by officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
For the most part, when airports were established they were located in relatively undeveloped areas, but because of the growth of most Canadian communities urban development has surrounded the airport. In recent years there have been marked changes in the size of aircraft and in the type of engines they use. These changes in themselves have a long-term effect on residential property in the vicinity, particularly in the areas at the end of runways.
The Department of Transport already has regulations and many municipalities have their own zoning requirements. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation must concern itself with the mortgage value of the properties on which they approve loans. After a study of all the aspects of the problem it has been decided that loans under the National Housing Act will not be made available within the rectangular area extending 5,000 feet from the end of a runway, and 1,000 feet on either side of a line that is a projection of the centre line of the runway; nor are loans to be approved within 1,000 feet from the side of a runway.
While the dimensions I have mentioned might at first appear to include large areas, hon. members will realize that in the larger airports there is a considerable distance between the end of the runway and the airport boundary. Similarly, the clearance from the side of a runway to the boundary is fairly extensive.
The restriction I have mentioned will have application to our main commercial airports
and some of the military airfields, but will not apply in respect of small or secondary airports which are not likely to be substantially developed in the future. A list of the airports to which these restrictions apply is being worked out between officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the Department of Transport so that there will be no misunderstanding in respect of airports to which the restrictions apply.

speechtext:
wish to rise to a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, arising out of an answer given to me by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) on Friday last, a portion of which was inaudible to me. The question appears on page 403 of Hansard of January 21, 1955, and reads as follows:
I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce arising out of the latest crop report and having to do with the sale of wheat. Why is it that in the first four months of the current crop year Canada's shipments of wheat abroad have dropped compared with increases on the part of the other three great producing countries? Why is it that Canada's share of the over-all market has dropped while the share of three other countries has increased?
The minister replied as follows:
The facts as stated by my hon. friend are not true.
Now, sir, I wish to refer to a publication by the bureau of statistics. Perhaps the minister misunderstood my question, but if he did not these are the facts according to the latest report issued by the dominion bureau of statistics on January 13, 1955. The answer to the first question is summarized by the Canadian Press as follows:
All major grain growing countries except Canada showed increased wheat exports in the first four months of the current crop year.
Canada's shipments dropped in the four months by 6,100,000 bushels to 97,300,000 from 103,400,000 last year, the bureau of statistics reported Monday.
United States exports increased to 72,500,000 from 70,000,000; Argentina to 45,200,000 from 43,200,000 and Australia to 26,700,000 from 22,000,000.
Thus, there was a decline in Canada's share of the over-all market with exports from the four countries rising in the four months to 241,700,000 bushels from 238,600,000 last year.

Questions
In so far as shipments are concerned, I have before me the bureau of statistics bulletin, volume 24, No. 9, dated January 13, 1955, in which the following appeared. It compares the dollar value of wheat exported from Canada between January and November 1954 as compared to the same period in 1953. It shows that the total amount of wheat exported in that period in 1953 amounted to $530,903,000, as compared to $339,871,000 in 1954, a fall in the dollar value of exports of $191,032 for wheat.
However, one has also to take into account wheat flour in the same period of time. According to the dominion bureau of statistics the exports of wheat flour from Canada fell from $93,590,000 in 1953, that is between January and November, to $81,371,000 for the same period in 1954.

The house resumed, from Friday, January 21, consideration of the motion of Mr. Pearson:
That it is expedient that the houses of parliament do approve the protocol to the North Atlantic treaty on the accession of the Federal Republic of Germany, signed by Canada at Paris on October 23, 1954, and that this house do approve the same.

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF PROTOCOL ON ACCESSION OF FEDERAL REPUBLIC OF GERMANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in continuing my remarks on this resolution, commenced last Friday evening, I rise to support the views expressed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, (Mr. Knowles) and for similar reasons, which he so clearly outlined to the house at that time. Like him, I am confident that we are expressing the views and fears of many good and patriotic Canadians. Letters I have received, conversations I have had with many people who are supporters of all parties in this house, clearly indicate very strong opposition in Canada at this time to German rearmament. At best, Mr. Speaker, there is no enthusiasm in the house or in the country.
I fully appreciate the difficulties, the doubts, the fears that this problem presents to hon. members, and I sincerely respect the views of those who do not agree with me. In fact, Mr. Speaker, I think the level, the tenor, of this debate is a good indication of the firmness and strength of our democratic and parliamentary institutions.
My opposition to this resolution is based mainly on two grounds: First, my fear of a rearmed Germany. I am afraid, as are many Canadians, of what a rearmed Germany herself may do in the future. Second, that in this step we will increase the danger of war because it is an irrevocable step, deepening the division, as I see it, between the east and the west.
North Atlantic Treaty
My fears of German rearmament and the fears of a good number of Canadians stem from the evidence that nazi elements are still too strong in Germany to place arms in their hands and the further danger of the revival of Prussian militarism, not necessarily associated with nazism. I have done my best to study every aspect of this problem and to read the opinions of those qualified to assess this situation. I have read a great deal on the subject and heard the opinions of those who speak with some experience and some knowledge of it, and in support of my argument I want first of all to quote from the Toronto Daily Star of September 29, 1954, the reported opinions of Rabbi Abraham Feinberg of Holy Blossom Temple, a powerful and highly respected figure in the Jewish community in Canada. The article, which is entitled "Lessons of History Flouted if Germany Rearmed-Feinberg", reads:
Rabbi Abraham Feinberg of Holy Blossom Temple charged today that in rearming Germany the west "flouts the bitter lessons of recent history" and that the treatment by the western powers of Israel as compared with Germany "is a shocking example of human error, a tragic betrayal of the ideals for which vast blood and treasure were spent in world war II, and a dire threat to peace".
"In the 1930's", he said, "western policy makers, urged by London, acquiesced in Germany rearming, as a defence against communism-with the ultimate and evil fruit of Hitlerism and unparalleled slaughter. Now, in the 1950's, western leaders, for the same reason, are being pressed by the U.S. into the same deadend of illusion, self-deception and fateful peril for all mankind".
Referring to nazi atrocities in world war n. Rabbi Feinberg said, "It would be suicidal to forget the bestiality of German nazis . . . the blithe, optimistic, carefree romance of the western powers with West Germany is a travesty on mature political thinking and a form of self-inflicted blindness which can lead all humanity to an abyss".
He said that many former top nazis now hold positions of influence in West Germany and named the following. Dr. Schroeder, federal minister of the interior, (formerly a member of the S.A. and legal adviser to Schacht); Dr. Theodor Oberlander, minister of refugee affairs, (who was an S.S. major until 1953, when he fell out with Himmler); Dr. Victor Emanuel Preusker, minister of housing, (an S.S. instructor on race relations); Hans Globke, state secretary of the federal chancellery, (who wrote the official commentary on the Nuremberg racial laws): Waldemar Kraft, minister without portfolio, (who did much to pave the way for Hitler's invasion of Poland).
The growth of new nazi splinter groups, the numerous articles in West German papers glorifying nazi leaders, the Nauman plot exposure, the prolonged campaign for the release of "martyred" war criminals, the frequent desecration of Jewish cemeteries and the belligerent diatribes of ultranationalist spokesmen-all these ominous developments do not support Dr. Adenauer's assertion that there has been no nazi revival in Germany. Throughout provincial and federal governments nazi membership is now practically a qualification for a position of public trust.

North Atlantic Treaty
Adenauer may soon become a venerated, powerless "wooden statue", like old man Hindenburg before Hitler, and the itch to retrieve heroic Teuton horror will soon be stirring in the German "superman's breast". Eabbi Feinberg stated.
"The German 'problem child' is of special concern to Jews", he said. The massacre of six million Jews by the nazis raised our casualties in world war II to a proportion of 25 per cent-far higher than those of any other people. We are entitled to feel intensely about the trend of moral and spiritual development in postwar Germany. He said he was "keenly conscious" of the threat to the west of "the possible plans of the Kremlin for world domination". But the Russian threat is compounded by the danger which arises from a renascent and rearmed Germany.
Western civilization, under the pressure of U.S. foreign policy, seems willing to sacrifice Germany's moral rehabilitation in order that she might be converted into an armed fortress against the Soviet union. From the strict viewpoint of religion and its eternal mandate to evoke the best in human beings, such a program cannot be upheld. "As a practical strategy in a hard and bitter struggle for existence, it is a grave risk", he said.
These are the views of a thoughtful leader of unquestioned integrity which merit the greatest consideration and respect. He states facts that have a great bearing on this problem. Furthermore, I am one who is disturbed by the fact that war criminals are receiving rousing welcomes on their return to their homes by a certain section of the German population. I am also disturbed to know that war criminals are receiving pensions for life, including the time they have spent in jail. The time they have spent in jail is considered as time spent in the service of Germany.
Even the text of the final act of the London conference gives some cause for concern. There is a section headed "German Declaration-Voluntary Limitations." This is section 15 and it reads:
That the federal republic undertakes not to manufacture in its territory any atomic weapons, chemical weapons, or biological weapons, as detailed in paragraphs I, II and III of the attached list.
The phrase "in its territory" is repeated in several places. To me those are ominous words. What about the plants being built at the present time by German industry in Spain, in Turkey and with the possibility of plants being built in North Africa. I cannot remember the source, but I have read of a possibility of Krupps coming to Canada. I hope to God they never do. That is one of the points in this document I would like the minister to explain, because the words "in its territory" do not appear to me to offer much hope of limiting German armaments.
Another fact which causes me great concern is what is contained in the text of documents agreed on by the conference of ministers held in Paris, October 20-23, 1954, and published

by Her Majesty's stationery office. A footnote explanation is given in connection with protocol No. II on the forces of western European union, article 1, clause (a). This footnote does not appear in our document and it reads:
The special agreement annexed to the European defence community treaty is not a published document. Authoritative German statements have, however, confirmed that the levels laid down for the German contribution to European defence community were as follows:	Army-12 divisions;
Air force-a tactical air force of about 1,350 aircraft; Navy-light coastal defence and escort vessels.
What disturbs me is the fact that in a document published by Her Majesty's stationery office and laid on the table of the British House of Commons the authoritative information had to come from German sources. Furthermore, I think that there is in these arrangements another great difficulty which concerns many of us. The main hope for tight control lies not in NATO but in the Brussels treaty for western European union and Canada is not a member of that union.
I have read as widely as possible and I want to quote here from a source which I think is well worthy of consideration. I wish to quote from an article entitled "The Dangers of German Rearmament" by Professor C. R. Hiscocks of the University of Manitoba, appearing in Canadian Business of November 1954. He can certainly speak with knowledge and from experience. For the information of the house, Professor Hiscocks has been associated over the past twenty years with various international organizations. British-born Professor Hiscocks joined the staff of the Royal Institute of International Affairs, London, in 1935. He spent five years of war service in the Middle and Far East, Crete and Germany, and then joined the British military government in Germany for one year. The next five years he was British council representative first in Austria and later in India. Since 1950 he has been at the University of Manitoba as professor of political science. In 1953 he was United Kingdom representative on the UN subcommission on the prevention of discrimination and protection of minorities. He was in Germany as recently as this past summer. I shall just quote from that article at various points. Professor Hiscocks has this to say:
There has been something very naive about allied views on Germany in their crudest form. Towards the end of the war the secretary of the United States treasury proposed the so-called Morgenthau plan for reducing Germany to a nation of farmers or, as some Germans now say with justifiable bitterness, to a nation of goatherds. Industry was to be drastically controlled and reduced. Then, within a few years, billions of American dollars were being poured out as Marshall aid to rebuild German industry and re-equip it with the most modern machine tools.

The period of rigid disarmament when a German could be executed for burying a shotgun in his garden gave way to the present phase, when one of the chief aims of western diplomacy is not only to allow Germany to rearm but to ensure that it does so effectively.
And then again:
It is hardly surprising that Germans are sometimes scornful of allied policy. Many sincere and enlightened thinkers are highly critical of American diplomatic pressure aiming at the rearmament of their country. Whether we agree with them or not, their point of view deserves respect.
I have never heard so many or such strong arguments against German rearmament as I heard in Germany this summer. It may seem curious that this should be the case, yet the average German has suffered more from German militarism than the average Canadian or American. Antimilitarism is particularly strong amongst the young. Some say bluntly that in no circumstances will they do military service again. Many more are determined that a new army should be different in spirit from the old. Only a very small minority would welcome the re-creation of the German army for its own sake with any real enthusiasm. One man told me that he was thankful for every day that went by without rearmament, because it meant that one or more of the old militarist gang had died off and that the danger of their restoration to power had correspondingly decreased. This sentiment is shared by many ordinary German citizens with no political axe to grind.
The quotation continues:
The real danger of German rearmament is the revival of Prussian militarism under some thin disguise, with its narrow nationalist outlook, its arrogance, its cynicism, and its belief in amoral Realpolitik. Such a revival would be compatible with a sincere repudiation of nazi doctrines, because the Prussian military caste included some of Hitler's strongest opponents. But without any admixture of nazi ideals it would be a development sinister enough in itself.
Towards the end he concludes:
For nearly ten years Germany has had no army. This break in continuity provides grounds for hoping that the militarist tradition has been broken and that any new army that is created will be different from the old. On the other hand, it is arguable that the interval has not been long enough. There are still many officers and NCO's available who are just waiting for an opportunity to re-create the old military machine.
I think the voice of that gentleman should receive some consideration.
The argument is often raised that since East Germany has been armed, West Germany should arm. The obvious answer to this is, however, that any contribution that a West German army might make to western defence would, in my opinion, immediately be cancelled out by additional rearming by the communists in East Germany.
Those who argue for the rearmament of Germany emphasize that West German forces would be controlled within NATO and WEU. Unfortunately, however, the great danger lies in the fact that German nationalists want reunification, and recovery of Polish-settled territory and Polish-held and Russian-held east Prussia.
North Atlantic Treaty
There is strong evidence that extreme nationalism is rising. When Chancellor Adenauer has passed from the scene another government might ignore his peaceful pledge. Civil war, war with Poland, war with Russia, might result, or perhaps even a Russian alliance may be entered into. NATO consequently might lose its defensive character. It is conceivable that under such conditions NATO might well be drawn into dangerous courses and increased armaments.
As far as arms control specified in the agreements is concerned, it should not be overlooked, Mr. Speaker, that between the wars Germany evaded arms control, assisted by Krupp and other big industries that are now in much the same hands. There is also the strong possibility that communist countermeasures would likely cause the west to relax control and raise more German forces.
I very much question the military value of German rearmament, and in support of my argument I wish to quote B. H. Liddell Hart, former British government military adviser, one of the greatest military critics in the west in recent years, and the only British military expert who foresaw the development of blitzkrieg warfare by fast moving panzer divisions, and whose advice the British government of the time refused to take in preparing to meet the oncoming onslaught from Hitler.
I quote from the Globe and Mail of Tuesday, January 4, 1955, carrying the headline "Expert Attacks Defence Strategy". The report reads:
A British specialist in military strategy says that much of the west's new plans for defence in the atomic era are a waste of time and money.
B. H. Liddell Hart, a former government military adviser, claims the realism of present defence planning is questionable under the implications of the hydrogen bomb. In the event of an all-out war, he says, there would be little value in the armies being built up by the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, navies, ordinary bombers or air defence.
The only real defence is "the deterrent power of retort."
Liddell Hart, one of the first advocates of air power and mechanized warfare, presents his theories in a long letter to The Times.
Three things, he suggests, are necessary for defence:	A strategic air force of "superlative
technical quality and performance," an extensive police force and "fire brigade" forces of high efficiency and mobility, in constant readiness. "The supreme fact of the hydrogen bomb era," says Liddell Hart, "is that war has become palpably suicidal."
A "realistic" appreciation of the military factors, he concludes, could change Britain's whole economic outlook for the better, while also providing greater security. Big savings could be made in ordinary bomber forces, navies and air defence, since none is capable of preventing "a catastrophic penetration by "hydrogen bombers" or bombardment by atomic missiles.

North Atlantic Treaty
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, Liddell Hart completely torpedoes the argument in favour of the military necessity for the rearming of Germany for western defence.
Fear of German rearmament is well indicated in debates in various parliaments and assemblies which dealt with this issue.
In Great Britain only approximately 40 per cent of the membership of the house voted in favour of the measure approving the rearming of Germany. The Labour party, with the exception of seven members, abstained, and nearly 100 Conservatives failed to record their votes. That was no doubt attributable to the expression of public opinion at that time.
In France the same measure was carried only by a minority of the French assembly voting under great pressure and after a lengthy and stormy debate.
In Bonn, Germany, the matter has been postponed further and internal opposition to West German rearmament is rapidly extending from parliament to the general public.
In this connection I wish to quote from the Christian Science Monitor of January 19, 1955, under the heading "Opposition Mounts", and then the main heading "Rearming Tears Germany". The report datelined Bonn, Germany, reads:
Internal opposition to West Germany's rearmament is rapidly extending from parliament and closed party circles to the general public.
The initiative in all this is taken by the Social Democratic party (SPD) supported by a large section of the trade union movement. Influential groups in the Protestant Evangelical Church also have come out strongly against rearming.
In fact, general indications and reports from different parts of the country indicate that the federal republic is more divided on rearming than it has been on any other problem for a long, long time.
The main argument against remilitarizing West Germany and tying it to the western powers is that thereby all prospects of reunifying Germany diminish to zero.
The decision to take the campaign to the country assumes that the Bonn parliament does not represent the will of the people. The Social Democrats are organizing meetings throughout their constituencies designed to prove to the general public the "dangers for unification arising from the government's foreign policy".
The Social Democratic party has appealed to the socialist parties of the world, stating its fear of a rearmed Germany and urging every effort be made for the calling of a four-power conference on unification. The West German trade union federation, by a vote of 391 to 4, agreed to make a similar appeal.
I am not going to deal further with that issue, Mr. Speaker, because I am sure other hon. members are more informed on that aspect of the situation than I am.
CMr. Herrldge.]
Opposition to the rearming of Germany is expressed by responsible people in all countries. Lord Beaverbrook has expressed his opposition through his press in Great Britain, and expressed it vigorously indeed. I am informed that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) was the guest of Lord Beaverbrook at Nassau-

speechtext: We quarrelled violently on that subject.

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF PROTOCOL ON ACCESSION OF FEDERAL REPUBLIC OF GERMANY
speechtext:
-and I am sure Lord Beaverbrook expressed to the minister his views on that subject. In his last speech made in the House of Lords before he died, Duff-Cooper made a most passionate appeal against German rearmament. General de Gaulle, who certainly has not the same political opinion as has this group, has taken a strong stand against German rearmament because of his fears of the effects of German rearmament on the safety of the French nation. Thomas Mann, a great German novelist, a great democrat who fled from Hitler and who is now an American citizen, recently said this:
"The trend of world affairs is menacing, pregnant with disaster", and he warns that by putting "yesterday's mortal enemies back in the saddle the west is scandalizing the peace-loving majority of West Germans".
He should know. I expect he has a great deal of correspondence with friends in Germany.
Thousands of responsible and patriotic Canadians oppose German rearmament. I have received letters from, and held conversations with, many parents, wives and children who have lost their loved ones. I have also received letters from many veterans who have expressed their uncompromising opposition to German rearmament, and 1 shall refer to two, who have informed me of their opinions. One is a retired major of the Grenadier Guards, who is a resident of my constituency, and who had experience in Germany after the first world war, serving with the British military mission. From his knowledge of Germany and of the situation there at the present time, he expressed to me in no uncertain terms his belief that rearming Germany was a most dangerous step. Then since this debate commenced I received a letter from a comrade of mine who is now in Shaughnessy hospital receiving treatment for first world war disabilities. He said, "I am extremely glad to see that some of you people are opposing German rearmament". Sections of the Canadian Congress of Labour and other trade unions have expressed strong opposition to rearming Germany at the present time.

We have been asked the question: What is the alternative course of action? In reply, Mr. Speaker, I say that we believe that time is on our side. We therefore believe in playing for time as an alternative: time to explore further diplomatic possibilities; time to develop Colombo plans and further technical assistance; time to remove more of the economic ills of the world; time to allow the further strengthening of the democratic forces in Germany; time to work for the settlement of disputes as outlined in the charter of the United Nations.
As to that last point, I suggest that the United Nations should propose a deal by which a united Germany is admitted to the United Nations along with communist China, and that rearmament be postponed. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, and in the opinion of some other people who have given this question some consideration, if we couple with this suggestion the withdrawal of Russian, British and American troops from Germany and the satellite states, the whole picture would be greatly improved.
At the Lambeth conference of 1948, a committee of bishops of the Anglican communion-of which the late bishop of Kootenay was a member and who is sincerely mourned by thousands in my constituency at the present time-dealt with problems the church has to face in the modern world, including communism, and reported in part as follows:
Communism cannot be overcome by argument alone. It has to be outlived, not merely outfought. Under the Providence of God its truths will pass into the experience of humanity, its untruths and half-truths will be self-destructive.
It was my lot, Mr. Speaker, to be born in an era of hope. No one who grew to maturity in the years before world war I could in his wildest nightmare have imagined the horrors which have been commonplaces of the daily press since the first world war of 1914. The science which men trusted has given those mad for power a capacity for the destruction of body, mind and soul on a vast scale, one so great that, in my opinion, comparisons with barbarian conquerors are grotesquely misleading and totally inappropriate.
The generation of my youth believed in a fundamental rationality of life and its essential goodness. Most of all, it believed in the sure and certain progress of the human race. This false confidence was somewhat justified in the light of modern history, particularly by the progress made in the latter part of the Victorian period in the western world. At the outbreak of the first world war, I, who was a progressive though not yet 50433-301
North Atlantic Treaty
a socialist, interested in peace and always opposed to imperialism, never thought of war in present basic and total terms. It is the hydrogen bomb, Mr. Speaker, which has made most articulate our fears for the future and which casts its black shadow over any hope of progress except towards destruction.
Today we face an unprecedented world situation. For the first time in history no general staff can guarantee its government victory, nor give any accurate estimate of the cost in military and civilian casualties or treasure required to assure any hope of victory. As Liddell Hart says:
The supreme fact of the hydrogen bomb era is that war has become palpably suicidal.
On that basis we must consider this situation. In brief, the logical deduction from the experience of our times is that if we cannot get peace, plenty and freedom together we shall get none of them. To achieve these objectives is an indivisible task.
Mr. Speaker, I have given this problem my best judgment and serious consideration. That is the situation as I see it today. I have brought my best judgment and serious consideration to dwell on this problem and I feel that, in the best interests of this country and of the future of mankind, I can do nothing else but oppose this resolution.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate has been carried on at an extremely high level. Thus there is little that I can say after the powerful and lucid speeches that have been made in the house. I shall not willingly, of course, lower the standard of debate by being repetitious. Unless I can say it better, I am not going to attempt it. For that reason the house will understand if I do not speak for too long.
It was in 1950, after the North Koreans had attacked the South Koreans, that Dean Acheson, secretary of state in the United States, drew a parallel to Germany. He pointed out the danger and suggested to the free world that consideration be given to the rearming of West Germany which was then, as now, facing an armed East Germany. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), the distinguished hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the knowledgeable hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Pearkes) have given us chapter and verse with respect to the arms in the hands of Germans who are in the east. These, numbering nearly 400,000, have been paraded before us in such great detail that we can almost recognize the regimental identification. It may be argued-as the hon. gentleman who just sat down argued-but surely it cannot be maintained that it is a virtue for

North Atlantic Treaty the Germans in East Germany to be armed and that it becomes a scandal when arms are provided for Germans in the west. Nor can it be maintained that those in the east are good Germans because their arms are provided by the Soviets and that those in the west are bad Germans because the free democracies will provide arms for them. When the fourth session of the twenty-first parliament opened on January 30, 1951, at the earliest opportunity, which was during the debate on the speech from the throne on February 6, I spoke at length of the dangers of rearming Germany. My words appear on pages 114 to 118 of Hansard for February 6, 1951. There I discussed at length many of the problems which now face this house. The tenor of my speech was that we must approach the problem of German rearmament with the greatest caution and safeguards, and with the memory of what an armed Germany cost the world in blood and tears in two world wars. We cannot afford to chance it once again without adopting precautionary measures, safeguards and controls.
Those words bear repeating because they are as cogent today as they were four years ago. I then recognized the inevitability of the step we propose to take at this time and my emphasis was on the controls. Whether or not the controls will control as we expect is the great unknown. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) said, and I quote from page 369 of Hansard for January 20, 1955:
I do not suggest that we should ignore the lessons of the past. Indeed, as George Santayana has said, "those who will not learn from history are condemned to repeat it."
By those words he indicates that he is fully aware of our previous failures, in which he had no part. Thus we should be reassured that in this instance there will be no failure.
In 1952 the house unanimously endorsed the European defence community which provided arms to West Germany and upon which the French later changed their minds. Subsequently, the French endorsed rearmament by changing their vote.
The present debate has been a thorough one and every aspect of the question has been fully discussed. I am particularly impressed and I am influenced by the forceful, profound and powerful speech made in the course of this debate by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Cogent in its lucidity were the words used by the hon. member for Prince Albert to describe that speech.
[Mr. Croll.l

The effect of that speech has not been lost on the world. The Toronto Star of January 22 carries a Reuters dispatch headlined as follows:	"Thunderer praises Pearson's
Speech". The article reads:
The Times praises the 'wise and timely' speech given this week by L. B. Pearson, Canadian external affairs minister, when he opened the debate in parliament on ratification of the Paris agreements.
It says the speech 'provided one of the most reasoned statements in favour of the agreements which has yet been heard.
'Canada was one of the most influential members in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. And in all that he said in the debate Mr. Pearson held fast to the original hope of a partnership of like-minded nations, wedded to a common purpose.
'As he looked ahead Mr. Pearson made a significant contribution to the present talks in Paris on the proposed European arms pool.
'It was a wise and timely speech'.
I found that during this week end there was a wider understanding and a better appreciation of what we had been trying to accomplish. For many years the Secretary of State for External Affairs has chartered the course of our international relations with remarkable ability. He has brought credit, distinction and peace to our country and helped preserve the peace of the world. I have, of course, read the Paris agreements noting fully the severe and binding limitations, controls and safeguards which are contemplated and which the minister has amplified.
It has been said in the house that foreign affairs are always a choice of problems. There is no sure or certain course. Decisions are made on unproved assumptions, weighing the advantages and disadvantages with the hope of a good result. The issue of war or peace in our time depends on our finding the right solution. This may be our last chance to solve this problem, and I think it is our best chance. None of us can be sure. Time alone will tell whether the rearming of West Germany is justified. Standing as we do at the crossroads of our existence, we can only hope and use our very best judgment, in the light of the information that is available to us, that in rearming at this time an aggressive and tumultuous people who were responsible for two of our deadliest wars in history we are preventing a third blood bath.
This is a momentous decision which, for good or ill, may determine the fate of generations. What we do now is with the hope and prayer that we are avoiding a greater catastrophe-at the very best it is a choice of evils. I believe this house knows my back-

ground, upbringing and family tradition. Seared and burned in my memory are names that will forever live in infamy. I have had thousands of representations and many delegations which have made a very deep impression on me. There is scarcely a home in one portion of my riding that has not suffered. I am a man torn. I have done much soul-searching. My heart, instinct, intuition and emotions say no. My head, logic and realism say yes.
I admit that the realities cannot be denied. There is no middle or alternative course. Without this step that we propose to take now, there can only be chaos. With great reluctance and a heavy heart I shall do what needs to be done at this time, without joy and with the Everest of misgivings.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the present discussion, to which I would like to bring my modest contribution, is of extreme importance, and I firmly believe that everybody's attention is now focused on parliament hill.
Upon the voicing of our views, as well as upon the decision that the parliament of Canada is about_ to take on this question- much debated in certain quarters-of the rearmament of West Germany, depend, in my humble opinion, the future and security of our country, as well as the safeguarding of peace and democracy in all those countries which are increasingly proud to belong to the free nations of the world.
Within barely a quarter of a century, we have been engulfed in two horrible wars, both of them started by the arrogant leaders of a Germany hankering for power, whose unbridled ambition was to conquer the world. The German people, as the result of their leaders' ambition, came to the conclusion that they were a superior race and that, as a consequence, all the peoples of the world had to fall under their domination. The only recognized god then was the fuehrer!
I have certainly no intention of minimizing in any way the incredible number of horrors perpetrated throughout the last two world wars by our former enemies. It will be sufficient to recall the memory of those who fell gloriously on the battlefield, the memory of our Canadian heroes. It would be sufficient too to read once more the numerous stories of the unspeakable massacres and tortures worthy of darker ages which were the lot of those who had been crammed into con-
North Atlantic Treaty
centration camps. Neither are we forgetful of the martyrdom suffered by those of the captured soldiers of the free world who refused to abandon and betray their native land.
How many Canadian homes have known separation, worry and death? The losses sustained by those who mourn for a husband, son, brother, fiance, relative or friend, pitilessly torn from the love of their dear ones, run into hundreds of thousands. And this through a war willed upon us by the nazi hordes.
Following those deaths, at the thought that these dear ones would never again see their beloved Canada, for the defence of which they had just made the supreme sacrifice, we, in general mourning, damned Germany and the barbarousness of her leaders and wished for her complete destruction.
Why did these young Canadians, on which the country based its fondest hopes for the future, agree to leave behind country, homes and folks, to risk and give their life?
It was because these young men had faith in the future, that they wanted to prepare happy tomorrows, make Canada a country in which it would be good to live in peace and harmony, and leave behind the fine reward begot only by courage and sacrifice.
The hatred that Germany called upon herself has not been forgotten and no Canadian, least of all those upon whom these wars brought sorrow and mourning, can be asked to forgive and forget.
It is owing to these few considerations no doubt that quite a number of Canadians of all racial origins are not ready to give definite and enthusiastic approval to this proposal in which we are asked to ratify the agreement permitting Western Germany to rearm.
German militarism having always, or nearly always, been a menace to world peace, it is easy to understand that we should doubt its fairness and its honesty. Since Germany did not comply with treaties and agreements in the past but rather considered them as mere scraps of paper, it is easy to understand that we should be under some apprehension regarding these new commitments.
The unforgettable atrocities, the innumerable defaults, the treaties wilfully ignored, those are all factors which today explain the reluctance of nations who have suffered to forgive those who have so often been called tyrants.
What new guarantees have we should we decide to forgive the past and try-however hard it may be-to consign to oblivion the record of so much evil, of so much blood and tears?

North Atlantic Treaty
Is their word worth more today than it was yesterday, or are the Germans sufficiently smitten with remorse to atone, by doing good, for the immeasurable mischief of which they have been guilty?
The representative of God on earth forgives the repentant evil-doer, often in spite of his many grievous sins, because, he says, the Creator's mercy is infinite.
Must we not, at all times, use that last-mentioned maxim as a guide and he who repents should at least get the benefit of the doubt when his present or future good intentions are in question.
In my humble opinion, when we deal with that ticklish question, we must put our feelings aside and be truly realistic. Great Britain and France in particular have, more than we, been devastated and have lost an important part of their population but have they not reacted once more when confronted by the far greater danger which threatens not only Europe but the entire world?
What is that danger? What is that menace which lies heavy on peace-loving nations, which hangs over them like the sword of Damocles?
It is bolshevik Russia, atheistic Russia, murderous Russia, conquering Russia, godless Russia, which harbours the hideous canker, the destructive ideology of communism and whose deadly propaganda aims at nothing else but the poisoning, followed by the destruction of the souls and hearts of all who fall prey to that doctrine.
The communists, making use of every dishonest practice they are known to use, through recourse to cunning, hypocrisy, falsehood, have infiltrated every possible movement, including labour unions, in order to sow discord; they even have the gall to disguise some of their organizations under the title of "peace congress".
The communists up to now have shown by their barbarous deeds that they are international bandits, dangerous spies and the greatest persecutors of the church and of the faith that ever existed.
Every day we read with dismay in the papers that in the countries over which they rule they have thrown into slavery, imprisoned, tortured in the most horrible manner and cowardly assassinated men whose mission, whose calling is to guide the souls of others and to spread the belief in the Supreme Being, as if these men were the most wicked criminals.
[Mr. Dufresne.l
This pernicious and subversive ideology has been spreading even in this country where it must be admitted that communism has an ever-growing number of more or less conscious adepts.
On different pretexts they carry out periodic invasions of these parliament buildings where, following blindly in the wake of their leaders, they accomplish these little pilgrimages of theirs, dangerous and hypocritical, with a view to furthering their propaganda.
More than 800 of them banded together only a few days ago. They came to this parliament in order to meet the representatives of the Canadian people so as to ascertain their opinion on the point now at issue. For my part I took a few minutes off to receive them and to tell them, in a few words, what I thought of their doctrine, of themselves, after which I threw them out. I took advantage of this opportunity to voice once more my deepest religious convictions and to state loudly all my love for our democratic institutions.
These Canadian communists, who are afforded too much freedom in this country, since they are a constant threat to our national security, because of- the hatred they nurse for our system of government which gives happiness, peace and prosperity, should be considered outlaws. Now, then, when will the government adopt this urgent and oft-suggested measure and when will they prevent this filthy propaganda from reaching into Canadian homes through the postal services of Canada which, in this way, become an indirect accomplice to the overthrow of the system democratically established in our country? Let us face realities. Let us have courage. Let us apply the best preventive at our disposal, the outlawing of the communist party in Canada.
For the communists, the word freedom means abuse and it is more than ever time that the Canadian parliament be made aware of it. Let us never forget the sorrowful and fatal consequences of the complacency and indifference of some countries now behind the iron curtain and deprived of the freedom which is a source of happiness for those who enjoy it.
One thing can be understood or rather can be readily understood, when it is realized that all over the world the communists dedicate all their efforts to the service of their masters in the Kremlin, to whom they are blindly subservient.

All their devotion is dedicated to this foreign and dangerous power, at the expense of the best interests of the security of their own country.
No matter what conquering Russia may do, Canadian communists applaud unreservedly her machinations which are a menace to all mankind.
In this debate I think that Canadian communists who ask for a negative vote on the Paris agreements are guilty of the most infamous imposture.
Have you ever heard them lodge any protest against the steady flow of destructive arms to red China and other countries ruled by the Kremlin, arms which might sooner or later be used against our own country and our own people, which might bring us destruction and death?
These double-dealers, these traitors, through their wilful and unpardonable silence, are satisfied and no doubt happy to see that the nations which have taken up the communist doctrine, or which are made to put up with it, will be able to arm to the teeth in anticipation of further aggression inspired by Russia.
Their behaviour is all the more treacherous, traitorous and unpardonable that they learn of the fiendish intentions of their infamous masters through a spy network well organized by Moscow and directed here in Canada and elsewhere through embassies and consulates, as we have found out in the past.
What is going on at this time around Formosa and the adjacent islands constitutes even more convincing proof of the fact that we may, at one time or another, be drawn into the most terrifying and devastating war in the history of all nations.
Red China is delivering repeated attacks against certain islands still held by the nationalist forces of Chiang Kai-shek, in order to prepare the invasion of that territory. That is no doubt the first step towards global and total warfare.
Those attacks have been inspired by barbaric Russia. It is the prelude to its attempts, born of boundless ambitions, to dominate the world and set up therein its regime of terror, slavery and idolatry. As for communist China, it only acts under the satanic orders of Moscow of which it is the contemptible puppet.
Whether we like it or not, and in spite of the optimistic statements made lately by certain chiefs of state, a sense of realism and an examination of what is going on should convince us that war is all but upon us at this time and that the free world is now
North Atlantic Treaty
being seriously threatened. Let us therefore adopt the appropriate measures now open to us in order to face the uncertain, perilous future that awaits us.
It is most unfortunate, Mr. Speaker, that the government have not seen fit to convene parliament earlier so as to allow all representatives to give this matter their undivided attention. This is the most serious matter to come before us since the close of hostilities. Once more the government now in charge of the destinies of the country have, through this reprehensible attitude of theirs, failed to recognize the supremacy of parliament.
This new commitment on our part, which does meet with our almost unanimous approval, must not, nonetheless, bring about an increase in our military spending. These expenses are already far too heavy for the means of our small population who, ever since the end of the war, have been groaning under the weight of taxation. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) must give us that assurance.
He will also have to tell us, unequivocally, what would become of our Canadian soldiers stationed in Germany at the taxpayers' expense if, some day, a rearmed Western Germany decided to invade the remainder of its territory now occupied by the Soviet, in order to proceed with the unification of the country. Would they be evacuated from a zone that had become dangerous for themselves and their families who had come to join them, or would the agreement we ratified oblige them to fight with the West Germans? These, Mr. Speaker, are questions that cannot remain unanswered and about which the Canadian people have a right to be informed.
For all these reasons, Mr. Speaker, and being aware of the responsibilities that weigh upon us as representatives of the Canadian people, I shall assume those responsibilities and vote in favour of West German rearmament. Of two evils, we must choose the lesser. I, therefore, prefer to absolve a repentant sinner than to become the accomplice of those who have decided to pursue their international gangsterism, in order to throw peoples into slavery and idolatry.
As far as we, who believe, are concerned let us implore the help of the Almighty and pray for the conversion of bolshevik Russia.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, because of the far-reaching implications of the proposal that is now before us I hesitate to take part in this particular debate.

North Atlantic Treaty
However, for the very same reason, I feel that I could not justify myself in maintaining silence. Therefore at this time I should like, at the risk of further repetition, to express my own feelings with respect to this particular, resolution.
It seems to me that this is a debate in which the emotions of hon. members of this house are being deeply stirred. It is a debate in which our powers of discernment are being taxed and our capacity for judgment is being tried to the limit. It seems to me that we are haunted by two fears, the fear of a revival of German militarism and, on the other hand, the fear of further communist expansion.
The first, of course, is not without foundation. Twice in the first half of this century Europe has rocked with the tread of German spike-helmeted, ironclad forces urged on by the dreams of power and their leaders' fanatical sense of destiny. Those forces have not hesitated to drench nations in blood. We do not propose at this time to recount again the stories of brutality perpetrated in an endeavour to carry out their policies. We do not close our eyes to these facts. We do not forget the cost in lives and material, lives especially, involved in the defeating of those forces. That is our first fear.
The second fear, that of communist aggression and expansion, is also based on fact. Read into the records of this debate have been statements made by leaders of communist thought to the effect that world domination is their ultimate objective, and we have seen some phases of that program become reality. I do not wish to labour this point further except to refer to the constant threat felt by men in governmental positions all over this world.
Privileged as I was to attend part of the recent sessions of the United Nations general assembly, I heard delegates from various nations refer to the process of infiltration, intrigue and subversion emanating from and aided by the Kremlin directed toward the overthrow of constituted law and order and the bringing of increasing millions of humanity into the slavery of communism. All this in spite of Mr. Vishinsky's declaration that Moscow does not export revolution.
The hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl) likens communism to creeping paralysis or, in some cases, to galloping consumption, the virus of which is slowly penetrating into every corner of the world. It seems to me that communism is a high-crested flood that threatens to engulf the world. It is a power threatening the very existence of democracy and freedom. This, I say, is our second fear.

It seems to me that our prayer is not for courage to do the thing which is right; our prayer is for guidance that under these circumstances we will know the right. I believe that each and every one of us will do the right thing if he can discern what is the right thing. We have been carefully weighing the issues, judging the particular dangers which confront us, and we must register our votes and trust that history will confirm the wisdom of that decision or at least credit us with sincerity of purpose.
Just today I received a circular letter in the mail-I suppose all hon. members received a similar letter-from the church peace mission, care of St. Cyprian's church in Toronto. I call attention to it because to me it is rather misleading. I know nothing about the church peace mission; I do not know how many belong to it; whether it is a properly constituted group or just what it is. This letter urges us to take our stand against the ratification of the agreement and I should like to read a portion of this letter by the Reverend D. C. Candy, chairman of the church peace mission. Referring to a previous communication which he had sent to hon. members, he said:
The following excerpts from the resolutions adopted by the assembly of the world council of churches, which met in Evanston in August 1954, express the view of the great majority of Protestants throughout the world:
"We believe that there are two conditions of crucial importance which must be met if catastrophe is to be avoided: (a) The prohibition of all weapons of mass destruction, including atomic and hydrogen bombs, with provision for international inspection and control such as would safeguard the security of all nations, together with the drastic reduction of all other armaments."
(b) The certain assurance that no country will engage in or support aggressive or subversive acts in other countries . . . We are convinced that peace will be seriously endangered so long as the armaments race continues. . .
He adds this sentence:
We heartily support these views and urge that the efforts of our government be towards their implementation.
I am sure the council was expressing the feelings of the great majority of Protestants, as well as those of other people. However, I would not go along with the inference that in order to accomplish these aims and objectives we have to vote against the ratification of these agreements. I believe his views are erroneous on that subject. He goes on to say:
In the early part of last fall our own Canadian representative introduced a motion in the UN general assembly, which gained the approval of all the major powers, asking for the continuation of the discussions of the special subcommittee on the subject of the control of atomic weapons and by all peace-loving people.

The writer goes on to state:
It would be inconsistent with the objectives of this motion now to agree to the development of any large new military force, let alone the revival of a German army, with its criminal record. Continued support of the work of this UN body will have far greater possibilities for the promotion of world peace than the re-establishment of the fearful German war machine.
I would again like to place myself on record as being in opposition to the view that to vote for the ratification of the agreements would be contrary to the spirit of this particular United Nations resolution. I believe the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) made a plain statement in regard to the circumstances that led up to this particular proposal. Many of the things that have troubled us have been clarified, and we certainly appreciate that.
Again with reference to the time I was privileged to spend at the United Nations, I would like to say that I appreciate the diligence and devotion with which the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), as acting head of the Canadian delegation to the United Nations, sought and succeeded in bringing the east and west together through the co-sponsorship of the draft resolution on disarmament.
We hope and pray that further negotiations will achieve the desired results. I say that, Mr. Speaker, because of the tendency on the part of some to imply that we are now following a policy of provocation rather than negotiation. Therefore, like other hon. members who have given this matter great, and I may say prayerful, consideration, I feel I must, and I shall, vote in favour of the resolution before us.
