speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate on the resolution to approve the Paris protocol to the North Atlantic treaty, I am fully conscious of the extreme gravity of the decision we are called upon to make. Implicit in this resolution is the question whether or not West Germany is to be rearmed. This question is one of the most momentous ever to come before the house.
I venture to suggest that there is not one of us who has not approached this issue with mixed feelings and with serious misgivings. The black record of German aggression, and particularly of nazi atrocities, generates in every one of us an instinctive revulsion against the idea of German rearmament. Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, this is an issue which must be decided not by instinct, or passion, however natural these emotions may be, but by reason and logic.
For my own part, Mr. Speaker, my misgivings have been diminished and my
North Atlantic Treaty
apprehension allayed by the clear and comprehensive statement made to this house by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson). He has convinced me that the real choice is not between a Germany disarmed and a Germany rearmed, but between a Germany rearmed within an international framework of control and a Germany rearmed without control.
It is impossible to maintain a permanent power vacuum in central Europe. As Sir Anthony Eden said: "The question is not whether West Germany is to be rearmed, but how." We cannot treat West Germany as a perpetual pariah, an outcast among the nations, because if we were to attempt that policy Russia, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs has pointed out, would be tempted to fill the vacuum thus created.
Let us try to imagine for ourselves what the situation would be if this protocol failed to be ratified. I venture to suggest that one of the first consequences would be to undermine the authority of the Adenauer government in West Germany, the government led by a man who is at one and the same time a good German and a good European.
It was my good fortune, Mr. Speaker, to be in West Germany during September of last year shortly after the rejection of EDC by the French national assembly on August 30, and I could not but feel that the failure of EDC had generated a sense of disappointment and disillusionment among the Germans. Chancellor Adenauer had pinned his foreign policy on the support of the west and one of the pillars of the western policy had been EDC. When it crashed to the ground there seemed to be a danger that West Germany would lose confidence in Dr. Adenauer, and his government might be overthrown.
That, I fear, would be one of the consequences, and we must remember that in dealing with the West Germany of Adenauer we are dealing with a different Germany from the German empire which Bismarck welded together by a combination of astute diplomacy and relentless force. We are dealing with a different Germany from the Germany of Kaiser Wilhelm. We are dealing with a different Germany from the Germany of Hitler. From the West Germany of Dr. Adenauer Prussia is absent. I think hon. members of the house will agree with me that throughout the history of the German empire and of Hitler's reich it was the Prussian junkers and the Prussian militarists who spearheaded German aggression either directly or through their influence on the German general staff.
I would venture to suggest that the Germany of Adenauer could be even different

North Atlantic Treaty
from the Germany of the Weimar republic because I think experience has led the West Germans to remedy some of the weaknesses of the Weimar constitution. For instance, the powers of the chancellor are greater. Article 65 of that constitution declares that he is responsible for the principles of policy and determines them. Moreover, we know that the chancellor's position has been strengthened by the fact that the basic law provides that if the opposition wishes to get rid of him, it must do more than simply vote no confidence in him. It must agree on someone to take his place. So in West Germany today we have a government that is at once a democratic government and a strong government. I think it would be a tragedy for the west if that government were to be undermined before its policy of co-operation with the west has been brought to fruition.
Another consequence of the failure to ratify this protocol might be the driving of a wedge between Western Germany and the NATO countries and the forcing of Western Germany into the arms of the Russians. We have seen the tendency for Germany to draw close to Russia illustrated more than once in recent history. The treaty of Rapallo in 1920 occurs to one, as does the Ribbentrop-Molotov pact of 1939. I therefore cannot see any alternative to the protocol.
I come next to the second thought which was left in my mind by the statement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), namely the effective limitations and controls which are to be imposed on West German rearmament. As he pointed out, it is of course impossible for human ingenuity to devise absolutely ironclad, foolproof guarantees; but in so far as these guarantees can be devised and applied, they are devised and applied in this protocol, as was made clear from the masterly exposition which the minister gave us relative to the controls with respect to certain armaments and the prohibition of arms.
I should like to deal briefly with the reception that the protocol has had in one or two other countries which are intimately concerned. We know, of course, that in France the French national assembly has approved the protocol, albeit reluctantly. That reluctance is perfectly understandable. France has suffered the humiliation of three German occupations in some 85 years, each one of them more brutal than the last. While I was travelling through France last fall, the brutality of that occupation was driven home to me very forcibly by a memorial in the town of Auxerre. That monument is not, in the strict sense of the word, a war memorial but is a memorial to the men, women and children

who were taken from that town by the German authorities, who were transported into Germany to work as slave labourers and who died as a result. Engraved on that monument are terrifying sculptured forms of bent bodies bowed down beneath intolerable burdens, with a hand stretched piteously from the earth. No one who looked upon that memorial could help feeling how deeply the brutality of the German occupation had entered into the heart and soul of France.
France has good reason to distrust and to fear Germany. We can understand why the French national assembly rejected EDC. But let us not forget that the French national assembly has approved this protocol which is now before this house.
Reference has been made by several hon. members to the narrowness of the majority in favour of the protocol. But it is well known that the 53 members of the M.R.P. who voted against the protocol are nevertheless in favour of rearming Germany and that they voted against the protocol simply because they would have preferred the solution proposed by their own leaders, namely EDC. If those 53 votes were deducted from one column and added to another, the result would have looked much more impressive. Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, that protocol has been approved by the French national assembly because of 86 socialist votes. Without those socialist votes, given in an almost solid body by the socialists of France, the protocol would not have passed the French national assembly. From the figures that I have seen, I understand that the socialist party in the French national assembly divided as follows: 86 in favour of the protocol, 18 against.
As to Britain, Mr. Speaker, let me say that the protocol we have before us was largely the result of the brilliant initiative of the British foreign secretary, Sir Anthony Eden. It was largely he who, following the collapse of EDC, mobilized the forces striving for the unification of western Europe. It was he who produced a solution in the form of a wedding, as it were, of the Brussels treaty with NATO, out of which has come western European union.
Not only did the British government take the initiative in bringing forward this protocol, but in order to make it easier for France to accept the protocol the British government undertook a new commitment, to maintain troops in western Europe in time of peace. This is something which has been correctly described as a truly revolutionary act. By that action Great Britain has sacrificed, if you will, an important part of her sovereign rights in the cause of international cooperation and collective security. By doing

so she has given practical proof of her conviction that absolute and unfettered sovereignty has become an anachronism in our atomic age.
So, Mr. Speaker, we find that in both France and Great Britain these protocols which we are debating have been approved by the legislatures. In Great Britain the majority in favour was 266 to 6. It is true, of course, that a great many members abstained from voting, mainly members of the Labour party, but only 6 out of the Labour party membership in the house of close to 300 actually voted against the measure.
In the course of this debate a great deal of emphasis has been placed on the time factor. We have been told that time is of the essence, and of course one must agree with that. When one agrees with the idea that time is of the essence the thought in my mind is that we must seize the most propitious time. I firmly believe that time is now. During the past four or five years earnest efforts have been made, not the least by our distinguished Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), to bring about a strengthening of the west for peace. It has been an uphill task, as we all know; but now, when the French assembly has approved the protocols, when Great Britain has made the sacrifice of sovereignty she has, when opinion in West Germany is more favourable to it than perhaps ever before and more averse to militarism than ever before, are we going to lose this moment? Are we going to undermine this fabric of international understanding in the west that has been built up by patient and skilful diplomacy?
I believe we should hesitate, Mr. Speaker, before we take that chance. Indeed, let us try to strengthen the cause. By doing so we shall be helping to strengthen the defences of the free world. We shall be deterring Soviet aggression, and I firmly believe we shall be improving our chances of successful negotiation with the Soviet union because we shall be negotiating from strength. If there is one lesson that the history of the post-war years has taught us in our relations with the communists, it is that we derive greater successes at the bargaining table when we can lead from strength. This has been the lesson of Azerbaijan, the Berlin airlift and even the success which we have achieved in Korea.
If we look at the rest of the world today we can contrast the situation in the Far East with the situation in Europe. What do we see? We see that communist aggression is
North Atlantic Treaty
more rampant in the east, where our defences are weakest, than it is in the west where our defences are the strongest.
This brings me to what I feel to be the fundamental question, and that is why this proposition is being put up to us at all at this moment? Why is this question of German rearmament coming before us? I should like to answer that question in the words of the French socialist leader, Guy Mollet. Speaking in the historic debate in the French chamber, he said:
Why is the question of German rearmament posed?
The answer he gave was:
It is because of the policy conducted by the Soviet union which menaces the peace of the world, and denies liberty to millions.
Yes, I feel that the danger of war today, the danger of aggression, comes not from Bonn but from Moscow.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, may I refer to the very convincing speech made on Friday last by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) in reply to certain comments made by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy). This was an immensely valuable contribution to the debate. I felt that the minister demonstrated conclusively that there is no inconsistency between Canada's efforts at the United Nations to achieve disarmament and this resolution which involves the rearmament of Germany. We have always felt that disarmament must be under effective international control and supervision. I believe we are more likely to obtain a successful result from the impending disarmament conference if we can negotiate at that conference from strength.
It is clear from what the minister said that Canada is not speaking with two voices, not speaking with one voice in New York and another voice in London and Paris. These two policies are integral parts of the same pattern, two aspects of the same policy. The Canadian government is speaking with one voice, a voice that has been listened to with increasing respect and admiration throughout the free world. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the parliament of Canada, too, will speak with one voice.

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF PROTOCOL ON ACCESSION OF FEDERAL REPUBLIC OF GERMANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the second occasion since I entered the house that I have had the opportunity, perhaps I should say the temerity, to take part in a debate on external affairs. The first occasion was in 1953, when we were debating external affairs in a general way. This time we are dealing with a specific

North Atlantic Treaty
measure, and we are asked to make a decision as individual members upon the matter of the ratification of the German protocol.
I suppose one of the reasons the ordinary private member in the house hesitates to take part too frequently in a discussion of external affairs lies in the rapidly changing picture confronting us. When we realize that just nine years after the close of world war II the whole structure of power politics has reversed itself almost beyond recognition, we can appreciate the point I have just made.
Then, too, Canadian policy has changed rapidly since world war II. I recall that after the cessation of hostilities in 1945 Canada tried to get back to what we called a state of normalcy such as had existed in the prewar period. We demobilized; we withdrew from European commitments. Even though we perhaps realized that, in the light of world conditions emerging after world war II, such a policy was not realistic, we could not resist that deep-seated and almost subconscious urge to get back to the period of peace as it had existed prior to 1939.
In facing this issue upon which we must now decide, we can readily come to the conclusion that what we decide now is not a final or fixed solution, because both in Canada and throughout the world tremendous moral, political and economic forces have been set loose that no parliament and no country-and certainly no individual- could control by any decision made at any particular time.
I should like to emphasize at the beginning of my remarks that defence alliances are especially transitory. Any cohesive element that might lie within a defence alliance is dissipated or begins to disappear almost as rapidly as the ink dries on the signatures of those taking part in shaping the alliance. Because of the uncontrollable forces of power politics that have been unleashed in the world we are faced with a condition that, for any definite period of time, is beyond the control of human ingenuity and human understanding.
However, I do not have too much difficulty in making a decision on the question before the house because I feel that the question set out in the motion contains the only logical conclusion to which anyone could come. As I have listened to the debate during the last three days my decision in this regard has been strengthened.
NATO came as a logical development from the rapid disintegration of the UN following world war II, which had appeared at first to be the beginning at long last of a meaningful world alliance, including the powerful
[Mr. Dinsdale.l
U.S.S.R. After examining the circumstances I must conclude that the fact we were forced to take part in a regional defence alliance in 1949 was not the fault of the western powers, particularly those in North America, because we were forced reluctantly to take action for regional defence as a matter of collective security. This was largely because of the unco-operative attitude of the Soviet.
In 1949 the cry was that the western nations must unite for survival, and as the world situation has further deteriorated it seems to me that cry is even more urgent. In 1949 NATO restored the balance of power in favour of the west. I believe a logical development in that process, in view of the circumstances prevailing since the war. is the incorporation of Western Germany into this regional alliance of free nations.
As other hon. members have emphasized, in the changing circumstances of world affairs it is almost impossible to believe that at last we have France and the western section of Germany trying to get along within a mutual defence agreement. We must also keep in mind that, notwithstanding its excursions into military aggressiveness twice in the first half of the twentieth century, Germany is basically and essentially a part of our western Christian civilization.
Having said all that is to oversimplify. The issue is not as straightforward or as simple as all that. Indeed, it is one of the most complex I have had to face as a member of the house, and one of the most complex confronting the world today. This was revealed in the minister's excellent review of the situation at the opening of the discussion on Thursday afternoon. It is not a subject that could be presented in sweeping and simple generalizations.
I join with other hon. members, particularly those in the back rows and those sitting in opposition, in regretting that more information was not placed in our hands at the time of the original Paris and London agreements. I have been under assault, if I may put it that way, from certain influences in my own constituency almost since that time, and it has been difficult to answer queries raised and deal with criticisms made concerning those two important conferences without having the information at hand.
Sometimes we of the opposition are referred to as the paper opposition, in that we get most of our information from the press. I have found from personal experience that this is almost inevitable, particularly as government affairs become more complex. As a private member I find there is not too much opportunity to get the necessary detailed

information on a matter as complex as this. Neither do we have the opportunity to deal with the representatives of the various free parliaments. We must formulate our own understanding and develop our thinking from the information transmitted to us through the various paper means of communication.
I venture to say that members of the armed forces of Canada, particularly those who travel abroad, have a more intimate understanding of and a more intimate contact with the actual geographical setting where these tremendous issues are taking shape. Members of parliament have to depend on secondhand information. That is an unfortunate situation. What the remedy is I cannot suggest this afternoon, although I do recall that when I first joined the air force back in the beginning of world war II the slogan was "Join the air force and see the world", and we did see a considerable part of the world at that time. Any personal grasp I have of countries outside the North American continent came from contacts that were made possible during those days.
In spite of the fact that to a large majority of the house it seems to be inevitable that we must ratify this protocol, there are some who feel that at this time they cannot vote for the resolution before us. I can partly understand that reservation. It is similar to the attitude that prevailed in the mid-1930's, when a strong feeling of pacifism was the dominant sentiment of a good many citizens of Canada and in fact of most of the western nations. Our generation is saturated with what we might call a mixture of sentimental Christianity-because as fundamental Christianity becomes watered down it tends to taper off into sentiment-scientific humanism and social evolution dogma. It was a mixture of all these sentiments that produced in the mid-1930's that famous resolution that swept through universities of the free nations of the world and which said, "Under no circumstances will we take up arms for king and country." A good many students of those days affixed their signatures to that resolution because of the sentiments that had shaped their thinking and formed their personalities; leading them to believe that everything was for the best in the best of all possible worlds, and never again would there be any war.
The refusal to ratify a resolution as important as the one before us springs from similar sentiments, I believe. Just a few moments ago the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) referred to the belief in progress that was our heritage from the Victorian era; and that belief in inevitable progress
North Atlantic Treaty
still is very firm in a large segment of the population, even though in Victorian times, under relatively stable conditions, the wrecks of civilization were to be seen on all hands, particularly in the Mediterranean area. These evidences that civilizations do rise and fall only served to underscore the comparative security of our own era. It was not until world war II, when we saw within the confines of the western nations wrecks of cities, the debris of our own civilization, that our thinking in regard to inevitable progress was brought up short.
I remember that in the early 1940's, at the height of the devastating bomber attacks on Germany, the crews taking part in those mass raids, in order to provide a safety valve for their own emotional reaction to the horror in which they were actually engaged I suppose, used to refer to a successful raid something like this. They would say they had heard a newscast from one of the German radio stations which said that a mass raid of a thousand allied bombers appeared over one of their cities this evening. The broadcast would refer to the destruction of a number of bombers and concluded with the final sentence, "One of our cities is missing."
That, I think, underscores the problem that faces a good many hon. members, as we have to make a decision on this matter. We are now confronted with the prospect of total destruction, not only of the physical aspects of our civilization; but with the additional threat of what are called the ABC weapons the situation becomes even more ominous. Not only will cities be razed to the ground, but we are faced with the possible disappearance of soil fertility and interference with human biology itself. The hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron) dealt with this subject a few days ago.
I want to emphasize that progress is not inevitable, and trends for good or evil can be disturbed by the actions men take, notwithstanding Marx and similar materialists -and our own civilization is saturated with strong potions of materialism today. I heard an authority speak on the subject not so long ago. He was rather cynical in his observation, when he said he saw very little difference between the atheistic materialism of Malenkov and the theistic materialism of western civilization. The materialists would always have us believe in determinism, that trends are inevitable, but I believe that man is capable of rational and creative activity. The decisions we make here in a free parliament, as well as decisions that may be made elsewhere, can be implemented into action, can change the course of events so far as human civilization is concerned.

North Atlantic Treaty
In addition to the general confusion of a problem of this kind, the issue has been further confused by certain representations that have been making themselves felt repeatedly in parliamentary circles. I have had many letters; I have had many interviewers, all of whom have urged me to vote no on this matter. I have not had one letter urging me to vote yes. If you were to take that as a measure of public opinion you might be persuaded to move in the direction of the noes.
I am a little bit suspicious of the type of pressure that has been applied to members of parliament. First of all, it is highly charged with emotional content. It is not a rational approach to the problem at all. It seems even to have some subversive tendencies so far as the well-being of the western nations is concerned. It is an appeal to conscience, and that is an appeal that can always tend to neutralize the westerner because, notwithstanding the adulteration of the element of Christianity in our civilization, we are still pretty heavily saturated with Christian morality; and whenever anybody approaches us from the standpoint of a peace offensive we always think very carefully as to the stand we shall take.
I suggest that approaching members of a free parliamentary body such as this with a peace offensive is much like preaching to the converted. I do not think the North American countries offer any threat of aggression, and such propaganda efforts might be more usefully employed in quarters requiring a little more aggressiveness on behalf of peace. We are convinced that war is a scourge. When I have been confronted with this emotional, almost hypocritical approach, I hark back in my thinking to the peace offensive of Hitler during the 1930's, when he neutralized any possible resistance from the western powers by appealing to the western conscience.
It is largely, too, an appeal from the standpoint of fear, and it was Mr. Roosevelt who said at a critical period during world war II that we had nothing to fear but fear itself. The world today, because of the continuing threat of the international situation, is almost paralysed by fear. The other day I was quite impressed when I read in the press the story of the smog that suddenly descended over London causing the good citizens of London to fall on their knees in prayer, and in general distress and confusion thinking that it was the end of all things.
There is an atmosphere of fear in all the nations of the world at the present time. We are constantly reminded of the scourge of the nazis, of the possibility of the revival
[Mr. Dinsdale.l
of German militarism and the modern barbarism of nazism. I would suggest that this tactic of the appeal to irrational emotionalism was just the thing that made it impossible for the west to stand up to the threat of the nazis during the 1930's. The nazi propaganda machine painted communistic aims and methods in such a bestial light that they confused the issue-the old red herring technique-and concealed their own bestiality. By arousing this irrational response of fear the nazis gained the allegiance of many of the respectable groups in Germany. Hitler destroyed law on the pretext of saving it. He undermined free government on the ground that he was its only safeguard. He brought all property under state control with the explanation that he was the champion of free enterprise, and he finally opened the gates of Europe to Russian communism on the excuse that he alone knew how to fight it. As I have listened to these representations by peace delegates my mind has constantly harked back to the Hitler technique of the appeal to emotional irrationality.
This leads me to a consideration of what we are up against in so far as any possible threat to our western security is concerned. True, there is a possibility of revival of German militarism; but I think we are in much greater danger from the possibilities of Soviet aggression. We need merely go back to the record since the end of world war II. It is not necessary for me to recapitulate that dismal picture here; it is well known to all hon. members. It is the lack of good faith and co-operation on the part of the U.S.S.R. that has made this whole western defence structure necessary.
In addition to that, if you go back to the doctrinaire Marxist approach behind Soviet designs and ambitions you will find they make no secret of the fact that they are out to destroy what they call capitalistic society, and they have a method of attack that is very difficult to deal with because it has two aspects to it. First of all it appears in the form of a revival of czarist Russian nationalism, and second it appears in the form of communist imperialism. This communist imperialism has, to my way of thinking, many of the overtones of religious fanaticism.
I do not believe that the Soviets will precipitate an all-out war. That seems to have been demonstrated by the pattern since world war II; but there is no doubt, by the same token, that whenever the opportunity arises, whenever confusion and chaos occur, they will indulge in a session of smashing and grabbing that is bewildering to behold. Such was the case behind the iron

curtain as they absorbed satellite after satellite in the immediate post-war period.
Of course it may be they are hoping that according to the Marxist dialectic the capitalistic nations will be destroyed of their own volition, that the elements of destruction are inherent in them and that Russia will simply have to wait until we reach a point of disintegration and confusion, when they can walk in and take over. That is why I feel it is so necessary to preserve, to extend and strengthen the system of collective security that has already been so well established in the NATO organization.
Actually if you look at either threat, the threat from the revival of nazism and the ever-present threat of Soviet pressure, there is much in common between the two. I remember attending a debate in Hart House in 1946 when the topic was "Resolved that nazism and communism are essentially the same". I think the affirmative in that debate rather had the upper hand. Both fascism and communism are the by-products of despotism. They are the results of the concentration of power both politically and economically in the hands of a few state officials. Of course this must inevitably lead to the abuse of power.
In addition to that, despotisms, particularly the modern despotism of nazi Germany and the Soviet union, are completely amoral. Lenin declared himself to have no belief in eternal moral principles. Actually all modern despotisms, and especially the two I have referred to, are more dangerous than any despotism that has existed hitherto, because they have all the insights of modern science at their disposal.
I was impressed with the minister's phrase when he said that he hoped science might be used for welfare rather than for warfare. I do not think modern despots are using the discoveries of science for what you might call welfare. Early despots used physical torture as an instrument to ensure conformity. In some cases they destroyed the body. But now the Soviet-and this has been amply demonstrated-uses new discoveries, in the physiology of the mind, for example, to inflict psychophysical torture on the victim. The will itself is destroyed. We have seen pictures of the white-faced automata appearing in the Soviet courts and confessing in the very language of their accusers. We have come to the conclusion that not only has liberty itself been removed, but the very essence of humanity has been subtracted.
We also recall the campaign that came from the same source as the peace campaign, with reference to the use of bacteriological weapons in the Korean conflict. We have discovered
North Atlantic Treaty
that this same diabolical brainwashing technique has been used, that the insights of modern psychology and psychiatry have been used in extracting confessions from prisoners of war.
Notwithstanding this-and this shows the very amorality of the threat now confronting us-no state in history has been more obsessed with "righteous" faith in the infallibility of its policies than the U.S.S.R. It sends men to labour camps in the name of freedom; it wipes out minorities in the name of liberation; it puts millions of peasants to death by starvation in the name of efficient agriculture. If anything, and this conclusion has been reached by others in this debate, Soviet despotism is much worse in its threat to humanity than nazi despotism ever was. In this regard I am constantly reminded that to fail in the ratification of these agreements will further open the way to communist infiltration. That is why I feel we must move resolutely and firmly toward the furtherance of western unity.
Like most hon. members I have reservations on this score, and some of these reservations I mentioned in my opening remarks. We are dealing with forces and powers in a great many respects quite uncontrollable, and we are constantly afraid that anything we do will usher in a third world war which would be the final madness of the human race. I would emphasize some of the things already stated in this debate, namely the need for rigid control of the German military machine and also, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of National Health and Welfare have emphasized, the need for continued discussions on the matter of disarmament, because nations armed to the teeth are always in danger even unwittingly of precipitating the last and final destruction.
Canada has tentatively attempted a lead in this regard. But it is interesting to note that any reference to disarmament by the Soviet seems to stress the ABC weapons, which have never yet been used to precipitate war. The atomic bomb was used to end the last world war; that fortunately has so far been the fullest extent of its use. It must be noted that wherever communist aggression has occurred in the world it has been carried out by means of superiority in conventional arms. It is therefore my view that any future war would begin with the use of conventional arms, and if our Soviet friends were sincere in their desire for disarmament they would have something to say on that score. Western frontiers have been engulfed by a slow process of attrition by means of

North Atlantic Treaty
these weapons, and that aspect of disarmament should be remembered in any discussions that take place.
I would like to emphasize again the nonmilitary aspects of the protocol now before us. It was at Canada's insistence that article 2 of NATO was inserted in the agreements. Unfortunately, due no doubt to our preoccupation with other matters, there has been very little attempt to implement the economic co-operation underlined in article 2, and in passing I would re-emphasize that if the responsibility the parliament of Canada is being asked to assume means anything at all it is the need to go much further than merely implement a defensive agreement.
Then there is the problem of the preservation of democracy in Germany, which is of basic importance. Only in a democratic Germany can we have any hope of avoiding a revival of the nazi military tradition. As I have already indicated, despotism always moves in the direction of the abuse of power, and certainly a nation having the recent historical background of Germany is in great danger from this threat. If the present democratic form of government in Germany collapsed, and despotism replaced it, all sorts of problems would have to be resolved on higher levels of foreign policy. We have to remember that Chancellor Adenauer is a very old man, and the fact that there will have to be changes in German leadership will present a problem difficult to handle by those entrusted with the responsibility of assuring the continuance of the democratic way of life in West Germany.
Then perhaps the greatest danger of all in dealing with this problem is the compulsion toward unification. It is rather significant that in any settlement or peace arrangement we have been able to come to with the U.S.S.R. the question of partition has always been involved. That was the solution in Korea; it was the solution in Indo-China; and unfortunately and tragically it was adopted as a solution in dealing with the problem of Germany. These arrangements constitute sore spots in all these countries, and the drive toward reunification on the part of all these national entities is likely to be the cause of a hot war breaking out in future.
Continuance of negotiations between east and west is of course fundamental. Since the change in the personnel making up the power structure in Soviet Russia there has been perhaps a new emphasis which is of utmost importance, and which should be remembered in any attempt we make to carry on negotiations with Russia if there is to be any hope
[Mr. Dinsdale.l
that the present policy of containment might eventually be replaced by some reasonable and sensible policy of coexistence.
Summing up in the spirit if not perhaps the words of the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), we are forced to conclude that any action we take on this important matter is primarily an act of faith. The uncontrolled forces loose in the modern world make any other attitude impossible. Power politics turn the world in which we live today into a veritable madhouse. We wonder what Russia will do and what Germany will do. No one can say what the future holds, and perhaps even those countries cannot themselves provide a reasonable answer.
But I do believe we must continue to negotiate from strength. That has been the NATO solution, a solution which has worked most satisfactorily up to the present time. We must also remember that we are relying not only on military, economic, and political strength, but above all on the moral strength which lies at the very foundation of our Christian western civilization. That is why I say we must make this final decision as an act of faith. We must believe that the balance of western Christian morality will decide the issue in the long run on the side of God and on the side of humanity.

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF PROTOCOL ON ACCESSION OF FEDERAL REPUBLIC OF GERMANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened the other day with a great deal of interest to the excellent speech made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. To my mind it was a speech designed to justify the action of the government in approving German rearmament. Since then several other hon. members have spoken along the same lines.
I noticed that the minister glossed over the history of Germany when armed. He glossed over the fears and dangers that engulfed us during two wars. Therefore, like several other members, particularly in this group, I feel that I should like to place on record my reasons for not supporting this resolution.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has already given the house reasons, with which I agree, which cover my case almost entirely. I want to make it quite clear that I am not opposing the admission of Germany into the family of nations. That action, by itself, is an excellent thing. I believe that everyone would support it. I believe the German people would vote for being admitted to the family of nations. I think that has the support of everyone in this house. However, I object to the package deal that is now before us, including as it does the rearmament of West Germany.

My memory goes back to 1914-and it has done so consistently over the past three or four days-when as a young man in London I listened to speeches made by prominent people, including both members of parliament and members of the public in London. I read the newspapers of those days and the posters exhorting the youth to join in the service of Britain. We were told that we had to do it in order to preserve democracy. We were told that nothing less than the full flower of Britain's youth pitted against Germany would bring about victory. We were told then that the challenge of Germany, if successful, would mean the end of our way of life. I well remember that statement. We were told that Germany must be defeated and must be forever effectively controlled.
On the basis of those statements and promises thousands of us joined, thinking we were being told the truth. After a long and bitter struggle we won the war. I have not the time in which to tell you of the price we paid, of the youths who died in the prime of life, or of the thousands of others who were maimed and crippled for life. You know the history of that war. Suffice it to say that those of us who survived looked forward to a peaceful existence for the rest of our lives, having accomplished what we set out to do, namely to disarm Germany once and for all.
Germany was disarmed. But before long people forgot the misery of the first war. I could not do so. I still cannot because I retain the memory of the day I joined the forces in August, 1914, in London, with six others who were also about my own age, five of whom paid the supreme sacrifice at the Dardanelles. Those are my memories. As a personal duty to those boys I knew so well, who gave their lives for a principle, I feel that I now must stand up and speak in favour of the same principle.
As the memory of the first war faded we gradually relaxed our controls over Germany. Although she was not allowed to build an air force, an army or a navy, she managed to produce some fine fighter pilots through the use of gliders, thus overcoming the restrictions placed upon her by the victorious allies. She was not allowed to build a navy, but she surreptitiously produced pocket battleships. She was not allowed to have an army, but she produced a small army composed almost entirely of officer material that eventually developed to the point where they could take charge of a vast army. All this went on before Hitler came on the scene.
When Hitler came on the scene they had reached a point where they were again strong enough to challenge the democracies
North Atlantic Treaty
that had defeated them a few short years previously. Once again the cry went out for recruits to stem the menace of a new Germany. Once again, in almost the same words, the same speeches were made. The same articles appeared in the press and the same posters appeared on the walls of buildings in England-and I might say in Canada -and again with the same results. Our youth responded. Incidentally two of my own sons joined the services in the last war, responding to the call. I too offered my services in the second war, as I did in the first, serving in the reserve army. This time it was to be a final war against Germany. Never again would they be allowed to arm and menace the world. Those are not my words. They are the words of Mr. Churchill, the Prime Minister of England, supported by other prominent men in the democracies, including our own country.
Again, Mr. Speaker, after a bitter and bloody struggle we were victorious. The second war was far more vicious than was the first. In order to see how much more atrocious it was, you have only to read the recorded facts with regard to prisoner of war camps such as Belsen, the gas chambers and all the atrocities that were committed in the second war, and compare them with those that were perpetrated in the first war.
I am convinced that a third world war would surpass, in violence and atrocity, both the others combined. It is even conceivable that the use of modern nuclear weapons would exterminate the majority of mankind, civilians as well as members of the armed forces. I therefore view with alarm the emergence of Germany as an armed world power for the third time. For this reason I cannot agree to sanction the rearming of this nation after having, twice in my lifetime, given years to try to disarm it.
An armed Germany will not bring stability and peace to Europe. The history of the last 50 years proves that statement. History actually proves that Germany has been the most disturbing influence in Europe. On what ground then do we now credit the Germans with better intentions? President Eisenhower, Prime Minister Churchill and our own Secretary of State for External Affairs have told us of lessening tension. Both the United Kingdom and the United States are reducing their manpower because of the lessening tension and are relying more and more on their superiority of atomic weapons.
This condition has been brought about without the help of Germany. Why, then, at this stage enlist an army of foot soldiers? They will not be allowed to carry atomic

North Atlantic Treaty
weapons. We are now told we have too many. According to the experts, foot soldiers are already a surplus element in a modern defence system.
Instead of allowing Germany to rearm I think we should allow her to use that money to improve her own economic condition and the lot of her people. I believe building German homes would pay far greater dividends than would the building of a German army. The German people themselves would prefer an improvement in their economic lot. A happy prosperous Germany, to my mind, would be a more effective bulwark against the growth of communism than any German army could possibly be. For that reason there is a growing opposition even in West Germany to the proposal that is now before us.
In support of this contention that Germany itself is not in favour of rearmament I should like to quote part of an article that appeared in the Globe and Mail today. It is written by Dorothy Thompson, and reads as follows:
The rearmament of Germany was launched by Mr. Acheson in September, 1950, right off the cuff. Since then even strategic plans of how to meet a possible Russian attack on Europe have changed. The answer would be an all-out atomic reprisal-and the Germans are to have no atomic weapons. Thus the political stability of West Germany and France and the confidence of both countries in the United States are being sacrificed to 12 German divisions which, were war to come, would be worthless, but whose existence makes war more, rather than less, probable. So, at least, argues the growing opposition in West Germany.
In a few words, Mr. Speaker, that is the reason I cannot support this resolution at the moment.

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF PROTOCOL ON ACCESSION OF FEDERAL REPUBLIC OF GERMANY
speechtext:
It has
been one of the richest experiences of my life, Mr. Speaker, to sit and listen to the discussion of this measure that has taken place thus far in this house among all hon. members. I honour every one of them, and in so far as I may disagree with any I do not mean that to be any reflection on them. This is a most contentious matter.
One thing I wish to point out, Mr. Speaker, and which I wish I could get into the mind of everybody in the Dominion of Canada and the United States, is that we have been talking incessantly about the fact that Germany rearmed and fought. We have not heard a single word as to why she did. Not a single word has been said about the economic pressures under which Germany was placed. Not a word has been said as to how those economic pressures might have been removed and might now be removed, thereby removing the cause of war and probably solving our problem directly.

I am not saying for one minute that the Germans were not culpable. I hold no brief for any of them. Nevertheless, would you not naturally expect that in a chamber of 265 intelligent members some attention would be given to this question of the probable cause of world war I or world war II? I do not believe there is a member in this house who has not heard that a fighting war is the result of an economic war. I wonder if there is a single member in this house who has not heard that economic warfare brings on fighting warfare. Would there not be some reason to suppose that fighting warfare was brought on by economic warfare? It will be along that line, to some extent, that I shall aim to direct my remarks.
Many earnest people, Mr. Speaker, have asked me to vote against German rearmament. Many have told me that they would watch my activity and read my explanation of my vote. I feel called upon for their sake to give my personal reasons for voting for German rearmament. What I shall say will be said on my own responsibility as a member of parliament. My words will in no respect commit any Social Crediter in Canada, and that includes every one in this group. I support 100 per cent the position taken by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) in his excellent speech on January 20.
First of all I congratulate the minister on a great forward step in organizing a counterattack against communism. A counterattack far broader and deeper than this has been in order for at least six years in this country, and very little has been done about it. All last year 1 argued in the hope of getting some sort of organization against communism, and now we have one step in this respect.
One of the main reasons urged by the opponents of rearmament is that the Germans, as a people, are unworthy to be trusted with arms. They seem disposed to believe that the Germans are in some hereditary way peculiarly base and unreliable. They seem to assume that the Germans have, of necessity, been the fundamental cause of each of the wars in which they have been involved. I was well pleased with the realistic approach of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott). He indicated that a great deal of that thinking must be essentially fallacious.
May we examine the validity of the position that is taken? Emotionally I have much to set me against Germany. In world war I I lost nearly all the best friends I ever had, my university pals, who went into the service

and are lying in Flanders' fields today. In world war II of my three brothers who enlisted in the services, one fought all through the terrible scenes in western Europe. I had three sons involved, one of whom paid the supreme sacrifice in the attack on Peenemunde on the fateful night of August 17-18, 1943; that was my son Winston W.
However, I must not allow things like that to affect me. I am in a responsible position. It is my task to try to determine, along with my fellows, what is the best thing to do in the situation we face right now.
To what extent were the Germans responsible for world war II? If we can find that out, then we shall be in a better position to judge the validity of the contention that the Germans are unworthy in every way to bear arms. First of all, what are the causes of war? There are many causes, but we shall name five which, I believe, are the chief ones. The first is racial ambition. The second is religious ambition, and let that not be forgotten. The third is ignorance, and that
I	believe played a terrible part in this last war, ignorance on our part because we did not know the truth. The fourth is the struggle for safety, for instance boundaries that are easy to protect. The fifth is the struggle for existence.
Let us consider cause No. 5, the struggle for existence. I believe that everyone has an inherent and inalienable right to life. I believe every member of this house will agree with that. One of the great figures in world war
II	said that a child born in Tokyo has the right to just as good a living as a child born in Washington. There is no answer to be given to that statement. I believe we will all agree. I agree. The big question is how to guarantee the child born in Tokyo the chance to have the standard of living which the child born in Washington can have. We are not, in the main, directing ourselves to that problem and how to answer it.
Everyone has an inalienable right to the means of supporting life: food, clothing and shelter. This requires a set of circumstances under which, by his own effort, he can obtain those things. If in any part of this world we have any considerable number of people who are deprived of access to the means of life, then we have a situation which is a breeder of trouble. If people are denied the enjoyment of this fundamental right to life they fight, if they are strong enough to fight. And if they cannot fight, they die; they eke out a miserable existence and finally give up the ghost.
Access to the means of life is to be gained legitimately by delivering either services or goods. What services, what goods a nation
North Atlantic Treaty
shall deliver has to depend upon the resources it possesses in the territory occupied, and upon the number and nature of its population.
Have we examined Germany? Have we given consideration to the number of people there are in Germany or to the geographical situation of Germany? Have we considered the rapidity of increase of the population which is natural to Germany; have we considered their natural resources, or their need for trade? Have we given consideration to all those things, to see whether or not the Germans might be in an intolerable position? If we have not, then we had better look very carefully before we go too far with some of the items contained in this resolution.
Let us now consider Germany in relation to these fundamental principles of life, while we contemplate her history. In the light of all considerations, let us now seek the causes of world war II, from Germany's point of view. What were the causes of world war II, for Germany? Most people blame Germany for world war II. Let us begin by assuming that Germany was to blame, while we probe about in recent history seeking to assess the extent of Germany's culpability. Winston Churchill called world war II "the unnecessary war". It was unnecessary from whose point of view; Germany's? Or was it unnecessary from the standpoint of those who constrained Germany?
We shall begin with the treaty of Versailles in 1919. Germany was broken; she was bereft of all her colonies. She was burdened with a set of penalties impossible for her or for any people to sustain. Her war debt was so great that to service it forced her into disastrous inflation, ruining her property values. A number of investors, including many eastern European aliens- and I draw everybody's attention to that expression "many eastern European aliens" -swooped down upon her and bought up vast amounts of her properties.
The republic established by the treaty was feeble. Germany stumbled along, with numerous political parties, and a near paralysis of government. Two parties finally emerged as powerful. First was the communist party, many of whose leaders were eastern European aliens. Mark that. The second was the national socialist German workers' party. Faced with harsh alternatives, the Germans chose the native party, making Adolf Hitler chancellor on January 30, 1933.
Five weeks later Franklin D. Roosevelt was inaugurated as president of the United States. On August 2 President von Hinden-burg died and on August 19 Hitler was made both president and chancellor of Germany.

North Atlantic Treaty
Hitler issued a series of tirades against communism, considering it a world menace. Roosevelt, on November 16, 1933, gave full diplomatic recognition to Soviet Russia-now there is an exceedingly important matter-as the result of the activity and influence of Litvinoff, Dean Acheson and two others, very prominent American figures whose names I shall not give here, but which I could give instantly.
One potent factor influencing Roosevelt toward recognizing red Russia was almost certainly the more than three million eastern European aliens who had immigrated into the United States and joined the Democratic party, and who had made known to the Democratic leaders that they would support the Democratic party in return for having men of their choice placed in certain administrative positions of influence in the American administration, where they could exercise control over United States foreign policy. There is one of the most serious facts in all modern history.
The German government had at that time the responsibility for feeding, clothing and sheltering 62 million people in a territory about the size of Texas. How would hon. members like to contemplate endeavouring to keep 62 million people in Texas, or in an area about one-third the size of Ontario? That was the task the German government faced in those days. I would like my hon. friends of the C.C.F., whose earnest remarks I honour, to ask themselves what they would do if they had a group of their own people in cha-ge of Germany under conditions of that i Ind. I would ask those members to think It through and not give just some careless opinion, such as ordinarily they give to Uf.
Germany began to implement a policy which might be characterized as Germany for the Germans. It was a policy which in some respects might be likened to the more recent policy of Mossadegh in Iran, relative to British control of the Iranian oil industry. In effect Mossadegh said, "These oil reserves belong to us. Let us control them. These people have come in here and built industries from which they derive the benefit, and from which we derive nothing. Let us see that we get adequate returns from these industries."
This pro-German policy of the German government naturally was opposed by the non-German stock numbering about 510,000 in 1933. In particular it was opposed by those who were eastern European aliens- mark that again-many of whom were communists. Most of these aliens had bought German property in 1923, greatly to the
rMr. Blackmore.]
detriment of Germany. Naturally these nonGerman aliens were unwilling to lose through the government's action any degree of their position of financial and other power acquired in large measure during Germany's hour of deep distress, occasioned by the famous German inflation and collapse of 1923. These non-German	aliens-communists-therefore
appealed to certain of their friends with influence in New York and elsewhere. Once again I ask my C.C.F. friends what they would have done, had they been in office.
In 1933 an international boycott was organized by these friends in New York to bring Germany to her knees, or to terms. Instructions went out to all friends of these nonGerman aliens of eastern European origin and loyalty, largely communists, that first, they should buy no goods made in Germany. Again I ask my C.C.F. friends, what would you have done under conditions like that? The second instruction was that they should refuse to deal with any merchant or shopkeeper who was selling any German-made goods. The third was that they should refuse to buy any goods from anyone employing German ships or shipping. Once again, what would my C.C.F. friends have done had they been in charge of the country when that happened? Think it through.
Arrangements were made by these aliens of eastern European origin, largely communists, to extend the boycott to include France, Holland, Belgium, Britain, Poland, Czechoslovakia and other lands even as far away as Egypt and Finland. They did the job up pretty thoroughly, did they not? A C.C.F. government in charge of that country would have been facing real trouble, would it not?
In connection with the boycott, the antiGerman campaign that had been going on steadily in the United States ever since world war I suddenly broke out with great violence, almost as though it had caught fire. Who was behind that? Germany was denounced in several influential New York newspapers, as well as over the radio. In saying this I am just recounting history, and recording the facts as they occurred. I am making no comment and offering no interpretation of the facts.
The public were dazed by all this propaganda. The United States government soon placed upon German imports her general tariff rates instead of the lower most-favourednation rates which all other nations enjoyed. What would you have done about that? This measure slowed down German imports into the United States, but did not stop Germany from manufacturing export goods. The United States then took a further step. She raised her duties against German goods by amounts

ranging from 22 per cent to 56 per cent in addition, mind you, to having placed German goods under the general tariff. Within about six months this measure caused German exports to the United States to dwindle to practically the vanishing point.
Next, certain anti-German, presumably communist, international financial interests made an effort to call sufficient German treasury notes to break Germany. Men in the house with financial experience will readily recognize what that was. The German government successfully met this manoeuvre by giving a substantial bonus above the current exchange rate to all foreigners who would come to Germany, exchange their currency for German marks and spend the marks there.
Germany made great preparations for welcoming strangers to such gatherings as the world conference on recreation and leisure time in Hamburg in August, 1936. Special trains of school children came from as far away as northern Norway. Visitors were shown every courtesy. The result was that tourists spent enough in Germany to keep the German mark stable. That was an extreme measure adopted to meet an extreme situation, over which a C.C.F. government in Germany could have no control.

Any time my hon. friend wants to enter into a debate with me on the floor of the house he is welcome to it. Evidently I am getting quite close to some place that hurts.
But this did not supply the increasing need of the 62 million German people for various* raw materials and other imports from abroad, such as wheat. These imports Germany could buy and pay for only with exports, which exports she was forbidden or prevented from making by those measures I have already referred to. Roosevelt continued his policy of economic warfare upon Germany; yet in his public utterances for some time he kept up talk about a policy of nonintervention in the internal affairs of foreign nations. In two speeches in the summer of 1937 he said:
Our national determination to keep free from foreign wars and foreign entanglements.
North Atlantic Treaty
Those were his words, but a few months later Roosevelt made a complete about-face, probably the most complete in the whole history of United States foreign policy, a very important matter leading up to the war. On October 5 in Chicago he delivered his famous quarantine speech. Let me quote:
... let no one imagine that America will escape, that America may expect mercy, that this western hemisphere will not be attacked.
When an epidemic of physical disease starts to spread, the community approves and joins in a quarantine of the patients in order to protect the health of the community against the spread of the disease.
That was a most important speech. In the United States the speech was considered most inflammatory and provocative of war. It caused unprecedented consternation among people in the United States. Certain newspapers outspokenly opposed the quarantine speech. Chief among these was the Chicago Tribune. The communist New Masses enthusiastically favoured it. I wonder why. Earl Browder, a national communist leader in the United States, was so highly pleased with it that he promised the Roosevelt administration the "100 per cent unconditional support of the communist party", provided Roosevelt adopted a hands-off policy toward communism. The majority of United States people called for clarification of the quarantine speech. What did it all mean? No explanation was given. The conclusion most people believed obvious was that the speech referred to Germany and Japan.
The German government, first in 1937 and again in 1938, made "a sincere effort to improve relations with the United States, only to be rebuffed". The United States government gave as its reason "a fear of domestic political reactions in this country unfavourable to the administration". Germany was told that the American public would not tolerate a conference. The Roosevelt administration blocked Germany's further efforts for peace by withdrawing the United States ambassador from Berlin, thus peremptorily preventing future negotiations. Germany was then forced to withdraw her ambassador, "who was personally friendly to America".
Through censorship the United States public for more than ten years were kept from knowing anything about these appeals and their sequences. That was in America the free! Even then the facts were ferreted out and made known only by the un-American activities committee.
Being thus economically strangled by an international boycott, headed in New York, the Germans in the late 1930's had to provide work for their unemployed by hiring them on government-sponsored projects, including

North Atlantic Treaty
armament factories. The series of events I have just related, together with the reactions Germany met in countries around her, convinced the Germans that they were the victims of "encirclement" on the part of Britain, France, United States and Soviet Russia. This caused the Germans to make the deal with the Soviet union in August, 1939, to partition Poland. This move directly precipitated world war II.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the house took recess I indicated by my remarks that much of the blame for world war II must be fastened upon the United States, the communist party, particularly great international figures who played prominent parts in the communist party, and President Roosevelt, president of the United States from 1933 on.
I mentioned serious economic pressures under which debtor nations are placed in the conditions which surround them in the world today. Strangely enough the creditor nations are not so seriously suffering from these pressures, but the debtor nations who most need assistance are suffering. I shall aim to refer particularly to a number of them in a minute or two.
Before recess I made a number of statements of tremendous importance. I realize how serious the statements were and I made them deliberately. I would not have made them if I had not ample evidence in support of everything I said. These facts are important not only for appraising the past and the present, but for planning for the future. If we desire honestly to build up a world in which we can be free from wars we must be guided by the things which can be learned, and which I stated, in my earlier remarks.
Those desiring to check the accuracy of the information I have given thus far in this speech will find all the proof required in four sources which I now quote; firstly, in the works of Dr. John Beaty, who I believe is probably as great an authority on these matters as is to be found on the American continent; secondly, in a book called "American Foreign Policy in the Making, 1932-1940" by Professor Charles A. Beard, published in

1946; third, "Design for War" by Frederick R. Sanborn, published in 1951; fourth, "America's Second Crusade" by William Henry Chamberlin, published in 1950. A careful perusal of these four authorities will satisfy anybody that what I said is moderate as well as true. I have referred to gross abuses of terrible power possessed by unbridled internationalists, all of whom appear to be much inclined to communism or are perhaps actual communists.
But besides all these particular provocations which were suffered by Germany in common with other debtor nations from 1933 onward, there existed a standing irritant that had been oppressing all nations other than the United States for a good many years. What I now refer to is the unconditional most favoured nation clause which was constantly urged and insisted upon by the United States.
The definition of this clause was first made in President Wilson's famous 14 points, announced in 1917. It is point No. 3, calling for the most favoured nation clause for every nation. The unconditional aspect of it had not yet been declared.
The most favoured nation clause called for in point No. 3 of Wilson's 14 points was changed to the unconditional most favoured nation clause by the United States in 1922, and from that time constantly insisted upon. If I have time enough I will give a little explanation so those people out in the country who read these remarks will be able to form some idea of the iniquity of the unconditional most favoured nation clause. Roosevelt's new deal administration demanded compliance with the clause, and this fact alone rendered the position of Germany intolerable, without adding all the other things which I have referred to previously.
Now I wish to say just a few words to the minister and to my fellow members of the [DOT]house. As I read the measure which is before the house, the only provision which is made to give economic help to nations in need is the building up of a set of vises by means of which we can clamp on every nation in the world the iniquitous features of the unconditional most favoured nation clause, whether they are able to endure them or not. If I am wrong the minister will have a good opportunity to reply, but I insist I am right.
What is the use of building up the United Nations, a central agency which will deprive individual nations of their sovereignty, without modifying those economic influences upon the nations which render their lot unbearable? How can anyone seriously contemplate such iniquity as that? Apparently that is what

the minister and the other planners who are working along with him have in mind. I hope 1 am wrong, but it all goes well I am going to give the minister ample opportunity to explain that situation to the house before we get through this year. There is just no use setting up a situation which is impossible.
We are led to believe by a wide variety of propaganda that all that is necessary to avoid war is to give away the sovereignty of the people. Take an illustration. We are insisting upon provincial sovereignty in this country, and in the United States they insist on state sovereignty. Would anyone in either of those two countries consider for a minute depriving one of those units of its sovereignty in order to place it in the hands of a central government, even though that central government were composed of the same flesh and blood, were the same kind of people as those in the provinces?
How can we seriously contemplate taking away the sovereignty of a nation, Canada, Great Britain, the United States, Germany hhd all the others, and placing it in the hands of a central power, especially when we have not the slightest idea as to who are going to constitute that central power, how the members are going to be selected or how they are going to be checked up and rendered responsible to the people?
I promised I would take a few minutes to illustrate the unconditional most favoured nation clause. Will you imagine two little countries like Czechoslovakia and Rumania, before either of them was brought in behind the iron curtain? Will you remember that each one of them is struggling to be sure that it does not import any more than it exports, trying to be sure that it produces as much of its own needs as it is possible to produce so as to avoid the dangers of international trade which would likely create international debt? We can fully appreciate that in Canada because of our adverse balances of trade.
These countries must have the needs of life. Czechoslovakia would be needing Rumanian oil, which that country would be able to produce in surplus, and Rumania would be needing the munitions or machinery produced by the Skoda works in Czechoslovakia. Rumania would be in need of those very things which Czechoslovakia had in surplus. Czechoslovakia would be anxious to have Rumanian oil just as Rumania would be anxious to have Czechoslovakian machinery and munitions.
A simple device would be for Czechoslovakia for instance to say to Rumania, "Now, Rumania, we will lower our tariff against your oil, we will let it come in at a much
North Atlantic Treaty
lower rate if not free entirely, if you in a complementary way will lower your tariff against our machinery. In that way you will get the machinery you need plus a market for some of your oil and we will get the oil we need and a market for some of our machinery. We will both be better off."
The unconditional most favoured nation clause announced by the United States in effect amounts to this: The United States says to any nation in the world, "If you lower your tariff against the goods of any other nation in the world, you also have to lower your tariff similarly against our commodities."
Let us see how these two little nations would find this to work out. Czechoslovakia lowers her tariff against Rumanian oil, and the United States sends in her oil, if you please; but she refuses to take in payment munitions from Czechoslovakia. Czechoslovakia would become indebted to the United States and Rumania would not obtain a market for her oil.
Rumania lowers her tariff against Czechoslovakian munitions, and the United States sends in munitions, refusing to accept oil in payment. Rumania falls into debt to the United States, while Czechoslovakia fails to get the market for her machinery.
We see those two countries thus put into a position which is ever so much more difficult because one power, the United States, has insisted that if any nation gives a reduction in its tariff to any other nation it must give it also to the United States. That is how the unconditional most favoured nation clause works out in action. When that mechanism is applied all over the world it creates a situation which is much worse, even intolerable. The lot of the weaker nations is made absolutely unsupportable, forcing them into debt and disaster.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what we as members of this house should ask ourselves is this. Is there any means whereby we can build up some medium through which we can bring the United States to use common sense in the application of the unconditional most favoured nation clause? We should also ask ourselves whether there is any means whereby we can protect nations with weaker economies. If there is not then all the talk of solving the economic problems and the peace problems besetting this world is idle and futile. An international organization which would deprive nations of sovereignty would only unnecessarily complicate the issues. In these terrible days when people of every nation are crying out for a lead my plea is, "Let us use our heads."
