Mr. Speaker, I feel it is my duty to declare myself on this issue, particularly in view of what I have seen and heard not only over the last few weeks but in the past few years. What I have to say tonight will not be quoted from a book, and the speech will be entirely my own.
I have received many delegations at Fort William; some of which have interviewed me many times. Most of them advocate the same line of policy. There was only one individual among them who did support the labour progressives, and I personally appreciate his reasons for opposing German rearmament. I told these delegations that I would not declare myself on this issue until I heard from the government leaders and from leaders of the opposition parties in this house. I have followed that policy. One delegation from Toronto requested me to ask the government to wait and continue to wait. He did not know my disposition. When I have a thing to do I do it now, because an opportunity comes only once.
These deputations urged me to vote for delay. I would like to briefly state five reasons why I support the resolution submitted by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. First, I support it because of the character of those who have submitted the motion, and of the leading men on the other side who oppose it. I do not require to name the two outstanding Canadians who support Russia. I do not know whether they are in the employ of Russia, though some believe they are.
When I compare the character, past record, influence, and service to God and country of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and the Minister of National Health and Welfare, with the character of these two men supporting the opposing campaign across Canada, then I can conceive of no better reason why I should support this motion.
My second reason is that since the last war members of this government have planned, worked, and campaigned for a permanent peace. I do not think that can be denied, and indeed it is quite evident throughout their speeches. The government want peace, and in seeking that permanent peace they consider the rearming of Germany one of the major safeguards.
My third reason for supporting this motion is the government's announced policy in favour of disarmament. Fourth, I believe in the efficacy of the rigid controls which have been inserted in the agreement with regard to the rearming of Germany. Germany
[Mr. Blackmore.l	*

cannot do just what she likes in this regard, and the minister has convinced me that the controls will be effective.
My fifth reason for supporting this motion is the difference between Germany east and west, or between West Germany and Russia, which amounts to very much the same thing. The last election held in West Germany was a free election. When did we ever have a free election in Russia since the revolution? There is one party in Russia controlled by one man, and anyone who dared stand up and find fault with their conduct of an election might not vote again. I believe there is far more to be hoped for from West Germany than we could ever possibly hope for from the east.
I would like the Secretary of State for External Affairs to answer one question when he rises to reply. If the United States, Great Britain and those supporting them had not stopped the communists in North Korea, what would have happened? Which country would have fallen next to the communists?
I have had some personal experience of communist tyranny through the arrival in Fort William of several families from Latvia and Estonia. One lady in particular is now serving in McKellar hospital as a nurses aide. Her first husband was a judge; her present husband is an outstanding lawyer who is now working in a camp, and he has made the statement that every time he uses an axe on a tree it is a blow for freedom. The other family lost everything, for they had to move out as the Russians moved in. Indeed, what was the use of being a judge in Latvia when the Russian government was in control?
There have been many fine speeches from the other side of the house, but the two speeches on this side which stood out in my mind and helped me come to a decision came from the hon. members for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl) and Spadina (Mr. Croll). I know something of what the hon. member for Cartier went through. Indeed, I remember telling hon. members that he would be criticized by those who sent Fred Rose into this house, who afterward was the cause of his own dismissal.
When I think of Russia today I recall the statement by a very distinguished man who, in addressing a meeting at Fort William, said there would be a revolution in Russia that would overshadow the former revolution. It is well known that those who come from slave camps in Russia say that all that is now required is a spark to light the revolt. Why? Those people have no rights; they are half

North Atlantic Treaty
starved; they are tortured to death. Certainly they have not the opportunity to speak for themselves.
Look at what is happening in Korea, with new airfields rearmed up to the hilt. What would happen if they were now allowed to go south in Korea? The result would be that South Korea would not be there, that is all.
It has been said several times in the house, why rearm East Germany and not West Germany? As one hon. member said, we would give West Germany its place in the North Atlantic organization, but would not give them their freedom. If we admit them, we should give them everything the other nations have.
For these five reasons I must support the motion.

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF PROTOCOL ON ACCESSION OF FEDERAL REPUBLIC OF GERMANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the reasons we should support the present resolution have been, I was going to say, adequately but I would prefer to say brilliantly expressed already by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the hon. member for Prince Albert and others, and I have no intention of taking up the time of the house by attempting in a much less adequate way to repeat what has already been said. However, for a few minutes I should like to comment on some of the objections that have been raised to this resolution by some of the members of this house who have expressed their intention of voting against it.
As I have been able to gather the four reasons that have been given so far by those opposed to this resolution are, first, that many have deep personal convictions; second, that Russia might be irrevocably antagonized if the Paris arrangements were ratified; third, that Germany must not be rearmed as she is a potentially dangerous nation; and last, as one hon. member put it-I believe it was the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre -the convention of the party of which he is a member had objected to it at a meeting last summer and had reaffirmed the objection a few days ago.
I should like to deal at some little length with each one of these points. First there is this matter of deep personal conviction. If a person is opposed to the ratification of these arrangements made in Paris on a personal basis, and if this opposition has been arrived at on a basis of reason, then nobody can quarrel with his position. Every one of us knows that one of the privileges we have in this house is that of arriving at our own conclusions after examining the facts. However, if anybody is basing his stand 50433-31
purely on emotion, without having thought the matter out, it is not a valid reason to say that he has a deep personal conviction. If the personal convictions are based on reasoning, that is all right; but if they are based on emotion, it is not.
As to the possibility of antagonizing Russia irrevocably, I am afraid I do not think this is a valid argument. From the things we have heard from the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and from reading the debates in the British House of Commons and elsewhere, I think we may safely assume that Russia is undoubtedly armed to the teeth as it is, and that she has armed her satellites to the teeth. I do not think we are likely to antagonize her any further by rearming West Germany. We all know-and it has already been reiterated many times in this house- that you cannot negotiate and deal with people from weakness when the people with whom you are dealing have the morals and outlook of bandits. There is no use in trying to deal with people such as that when that is the attitude they have.
There are plenty of historical examples, and I shall mention one or two. If you go far enough back, to the twelfth or thirteenth century, you have the case of the famous Asiatic conqueror, Genghis Khan. Cities like Samarkand in central Asia had tried to treat with Genghis Khan. They offered him presents and tried to appease him. He took the presents, and of course he took the cities and the people were treated very badly, if one cares to go into the details of what happened.
We have, of course, a much more recent example of what happens when you are trying to deal with a country that is bent on world conquest-admittedly so-and is armed to the teeth. In 1939 I think we all remember that in numerous European countries-and, I am afraid, in many countries which are closer than that-people did everything they could to avoid war. Germany was appeased right and left, and we all remember the ultimate result. Germany accepted appeasement and took whatever she liked, until finally it was decided that she could go no further, and that there were some things worse than war.
It seems to me that those who have been objecting to the ratification of this agreement have been bringing out this old line of appeasement again. In fact it is virtually undisguised. Looking back, I can remember the 1930's when I was attending university and taking a course in political science. I think most of us who took the course in that period became greatly interested in socialist

North Atlantic Treaty
same reason that was offered by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, I cannot help feeling that probably some who have not yet spoken and some who intend to speak will be objecting to the ratification of these arrangements, and that one of the reasons they will give for their objection will be the one offered by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
I find this a strange reason, because the decision reached at the national convention of the C.C.F. party last August was made before the present arrangements were drawn up. I find it difficult to understand how that convention or meeting could form a conclusion when the arrangements had not been made upon which they were deciding. I find that strange indeed. And the hon. member mentioned that the executive council of this party meeting last week had objected to ratification. Yet according to the information given to us by the Secretary of State for External Affairs it was not known at that time. Again we have a case of making a decision without knowing what were the facts.
I should like to refer briefly to the attitude of the C.C.F. party, or a substantial part of it, since 1939. I would point out that their attitude in respect of resistance to aggression has been rather out of line with the Canadian point of view generally. It has proved to be unrealistic and, if I may say so, wrong.
First of all I would refer to Hansard for 1939, the second session, where at page 55 the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) was setting out the views of his party concerning the declaration of the second world war. At that time he said:
In view of these considerations, the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation believes that Canada s policy should be based first on the fundamental national interests of the Canadian people, as well as on their interest in the outcome of war. Canada should be prepared to defend her own shores, but her assistance overseas should be limited to economic aid and must not include conscription of manpower or the sending of any expeditionary force.
And again on the same page:
No military participation overseas. Any attempt to send a force abroad would rob us of the manpower necessary for the defence of our shores and for home production, would gravely endanger national unity, would threaten our civil liberties and democratic institutions, and would ultimately lead to conscription.
And finally at page 57 the hon. member said:
We believe, as I have said, that the sending of expeditionary forces is unnecessary and unwise.
Then to continue on from 1939 I would refer briefly to an editorial in this morning's Montreal Gazette, headed "Canada's Bevanly Host". I shall refer to only a short portion of

it, in which reference is made to the policy of the C.C.F. since the close of the second world war. It states:
In fact, varying degrees of opposition have appeared within the C.C.F. to nearly every step taken since the end of the second world war to resist communist expansion.
When the Marshall plan was inaugurated, it was officially condemned by the Manitoba convention of the C.C.F. as being "framed to provide capitalists with markets, rather than to help the people of Europe".
When the United States supported the Atlantic pact (out of which NATO has grown) the provincial convention of the C.C.F. in British Columbia passed a resolution opposing "any further expenditures on arms." After the Korean war broke out, the C.C.F. premier of Saskatchewan, Hon. T. C. Douglas, said that the United States was trying to use the United Nations to protect the interests of certain oil corporations, notably Standard Oil. Under such circumstances, the people of Saskatchewan were being called on "to send their sons to be slaughtered in foreign fields."
I have already referred to the speech of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in which he referred to the decision of the C.C.F. national convention last August and of their national council about a week ago. If hon. members oppose this motion on grounds of their convictions, they are quite justified in doing so. I feel that many who have opposed it, some of whom I know better than others, have done so because of their convictions. But if, to help them in making up their minds, they are using some of the suggestions that have been put forward by that party in the past, then I would suggest that before they vote they should refer back to some of those decisions, made by either a part of or by the whole party, and carefully review what actually happened.
Sometimes party directives are issued and members feel obliged to follow them; but hon. members should see that those directives are based upon reality. I repeat that under no circumstances do I make personal reference to any member in the house. My brief history of the foreign policy of the C.C.F. is the history of a group of which hon. members sitting in the house form possibly only a small part.
Then there is another matter I should like to touch upon briefly, one that has not yet been mentioned in this debate, and to which in my opinion careful consideration should be given. I refer to the leadership Great Britain has given in the drawing up of these various arrangements. This is something that, as yet, has not been emphasized. I believe we all know that after the failure of EDC it was Anthony Eden-and I am sure the Secretary of State for External Affairs would confirm this-who was able to effect a rapprochement between Mr. Dulles

and Mr. Mendes-France so they were prepared to compromise in order to draw up the present Paris arrangement.
This must have been a difficult task. Most of us are not personally familiar with the intricacies of French parliamentary life, but I think we have been able to gather that proceedings in the French parliament are quite different from those here. There are many parties and great rivalry among them. In the final ratification of these arrangements in the French parliament we saw the communists voting against it, along with the de Gaullists and the M.R.P., who had nothing in common with the communists but must have so aligned themselves for purposes of political strategy.
It is a great credit to Mr. Eden and to Mr. Mendes-France that these arrangements were drawn up in such a way as to be acceptable. We know Mr. Eden has effected a number of brilliant arrangements in the last year or so. We remember the Iranian oil dispute, a great source of world tension, which through the efforts of Mr. Eden was ironed out. Then there was the touchy and explosive situation at the Suez canal, also worked out successfully by Mr. Eden.
We know that shortly there is to be a meeting of commonwealth prime ministers in London. It would be well for us to watch and see what happens.
Sir Anthony Eden has been very successful in easing tension in the world. A great deal of account should be taken of the fact that England has shown a resurgence of leadership in these matters. I understand that India, Australia, New Zealand, Pakistan, Ceylon and Canada will be represented at the commonwealth conference. After discussing the matters that are to be dealt with at that conference-we do not yet know what they will be-if Sir Anthony Eden is able to repeat what he has done in the last year or so, it may well be that this commonwealth conference will affect the whole future of international relations.
As I mentioned earlier, it is true that we cannot treat or try to make arrangements to deal with Russia unless we are strong enough to do so, because she will not pay any attention to us unless we are strong. If we are strong enough it may be that the diplomacy of the commonwealth countries will ultimately bring about a real state of coexistence in the world. I am sure that it will lessen the danger of war "to a point", to coin a phrase, "of no return", and we shall not have to worry about wars in the future.

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF PROTOCOL ON ACCESSION OF FEDERAL REPUBLIC OF GERMANY
speechtext:
It is not
easy for me to resist the invitation of the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) to become involved with him in a political debate, but the international situation is far too grave for me to take time to pursue a discussion with the hon. member tonight.
With very few exceptions the hon. members who have taken part in this important debate have set an exceptionally high tone, and I shall try to maintain that high level. The members of the press have reported objectively the discussions which have taken place in this parliament The Toronto Globe and Mail, in a comment on its editorial page this morning, said:
Dissenting C.C.F. members, even though mistaken, have performed a useful service by expounding the minority view in the debate which began last Thursday.
The first suggestion I should like to make is to recommend that this inflammable question be referred to the United Nations. Let me remind the house that before the second world war ended we spent a good deal of time in making plans to ensure that never again would the world be plunged into a war. We set out a worth-while goal in the preamble to the charter of the United Nations:
to practice tolerance and live together in peace with one another as good neighbors, and to unite our strength to maintain international peace and security,
And so forth. We have made provision to ask the security council to investigate any dispute or situation:
... to see if its continuance is likely to endanger international peace and security. Such a dispute or situation may be brought to its attention by any member or, if it accepts in advance the obligations of specific settlement contained in the charter by any non-member.
The council determines the existence of any threat to the peace, breach of the peace or act of aggression. It makes recommendations or decides to take enforcement measures to maintain or restore international peace and security.
The situation in Formosa, as reported in tonight's paper, is very critical. In addition, solving the German question is so essential that this matter should be referred to the security council. If the security council is unable to deal satisfactorily with it, I suggest that Dr. Bertrand Russell, in his article in The Nation on December 18, 1954, makes suggestions which should receive consideration. Dr. Russell said:
Mankind at the present time is faced by dangers to the whole species so great that the avoidance of them ought to be the common aim of all the powers. The facts are known to everybody who chooses to know them, but for reasons of propaganda they are not adequately emphasized on either side of the iron curtain. It is true that

North Atlantic Treaty
they have been stated in western countries but not in such a manner as to influence policy. They have been stated more clearly and forcibly in America than in any other country, but they do not seem to have made any impact upon the average congressman or the average American voter.
Further on Dr. Russell says:
There is, however, another alternative. It is that both sides should recognize, and should be known to recognize sincerely, that war has become futile. Neither side alone can be vigorous in urging the futility of war since to do so gives an impression of weakness. It is here that neutrals can, if they will, save both camps from destruction.
Neutrals have two advantages over the powers in either camp. The first advantage is that they can urge the destructiveness and futility of war without incurring the odium of seeming to advocate cowardly submission. The second advantage is that they can speak to governments on both sides without being thought to be actuated merely by bias.
Neutral governments, on the contrary, can speak in identical terms to both communist and noncommunist powers, and can avoid the suspicion that they are concerned to promote the success of either side.
Dr. Russell suggests that India and Sweden might be two countries that could be persuaded to act as a neutral commission to try to find out the consequences of a third war on neutrals particularly. He suggests those two countries because Sweden has its natural association with the west and India is most anxious to ease east-west tensions. Dr. Russell suggests that on such a commission there should be military, naval and air experts, first class nuclear physicists, bacteriologists, economists and men of experience in international politics. I am convinced that a body such as that could draw up a report which would make the futility of a third world war undeniable. In conclusion he says:
The truth is so plain and simple that it seems as if governments must in time become aware of it: the communist and non-communist worlds can live together or die together. There is no other possibility. When both sides realize this, it may be hoped that they will choose to live rather than die.
Therefore I submit, Mr. Speaker, our first concern should be to try to get all sides to agree that the United Nations should be given a chance to negotiate to see if something could not be done.
The second part of my speech of course must deal with Germany. We have had a good deal of discussion about sovereign rights, about the privileges and responsibilities of the people in Germany and so on. We should clarify our thinking as to how far we can go in giving people the right to embark on programs to build up armaments and participate in the destruction of the entire world. However, I want to make it very clear that I feel Germany should be recognized as

a country that has made a worth-while contribution to the world. The German people must be given the chance to develop in the future. We should remember our ideals as set forth by President Roosevelt and Prime Minister Churchill when they suggested that their countries seek no aggrandizement, territorially or otherwise. They desire to see no territorial changes that do not accord with the freely expressed wishes of the peoples concerned; they respect the right of all peoples to choose the form of government under which they will live, and they wish to see sovereign rights and self-government restored to those who have been forcibly deprived of them. I am anxious that people in Germany should have their rights.
There has been a good deal said about the fact that Germany is divided into East Germany and West Germany. We seem to have lost sight of the fact that Germany has been divided into four sectors. There is a part now in Poland and a part in soviet Russia. According to the ideals that were set out in the Atlantic charter we must respect the rights of all peoples to choose the countries in which they want to live, and I think the German people in these four sectors must be given a chance to live together again as a united Germany, as soon as they are able to convince the rest of the world that there is no danger of a revived militarism plunging the world into war.
In this morning's Globe and Mail there were two articles on the editorial page which I think deserve mention. The hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Jones) referred to one paragraph in Dorothy Thompson's article. Another paragraph says:
The rearmament issue is tearing West Germany into vehemently opposing camps. Spearheaded by the social democrats and the trade unions, but supported by non-socialists, including outstanding members of the Protestant Evangelical church, a nation-wide campaign is under way to take the issue to the people. A 24-hour strike of Ruhr coal miners, though called for another reason, turned into an anti-rearmament demonstration. On January 29, the campaign will culminate in a huge mass meeting in the Pauls church in Frankfurt.
Speaking about Chancellor Adenauer:
The weakness of the chancellor's position is that he can offer no rational explanation of how Germany can be reunited once the step has been taken to create a German army in military alliance with NATO. Neither can the British, French or American foreign offices. In fact, Germans are coming to the alarmed conclusion that the "peace of the powers" (or coexistence) is envisaged as resting on a final four-power agreement to maintain and respect the existing status quo. They are vividly aware that the truces in Korea and Indo-China were won at the cost of dividing these two nations.

Then another paragraph:
Can It continue? Is it conceivable that a German government and army can indefinitely commit the nation actually to defend the partition of the country? If, behind the scenes, the western foreign offices are preparing to accept permanent German division as the price for "stability and peace" would that not constitute "containment" of a rump Germany, with a German army actually collaborating to police the condition? If so, how much popular support would such an army have? And unless it commands popular confidence what good is any army?
George Bain, in his "Ottawa Letter" this morning said:
After the first world war Germany was not allowed either,-
Referring to bombers and long range aircraft.
-and only a very few German officers were permitted to take flying training. However, leading German aircraft firms as early as 1926 had for some time been producing planes in Russia, Switzerland and Sweden, and within the civilian firm Luft-Hansa, a training system had been set up.
Germany after the first world war was not allowed tanks, submarines, heavy artillery, just as today it unconditionally guarantees not to manufacture such things as atomic, biological and chemical weapons and guided missiles.
However, ways were found to get around the bans following the first world war. Krupps, for instance, had bought control of the Bofors arms factory in Sweden by 1925. Submarines were being produced by German-controlled firms in Holland and Spain, even in Turkey and Finland.
And again:
In 1926, a three-nations commission reported that "Germany had never disarmed, had never had the intention of disarming, and for seven years had done everything in her power to deceive . . . the commission appointed to control her disarmament." Because the allied powers so desperately wanted to believe that Germany had been converted to peaceful ways, this report was buried.
Today there is not only a desire to believe in Germany's peaceful intentions, but also a recognition that a rearmed Germany is necessary to the defence of western Europe.
I was interested in an article on "Versailles and London" by J. Alvarez del Vayo, the foreign editor of The Nation and I quote from the issue of October 23, 1954:
The measures adopted, and to be adopted, to keep German rearmament under effective control are a constant theme in commentaries on the London conference. They cropped up in the debate which preceded the French parliament vote of confidence in Mendes-France. They are referred to repeatedly in the praise heaped upon the conference by statesmen and politicians.
And further on:
Apparently no one doubts that the arms control agency to be set up as part of the Brussels treaty organization will be able to keep the massive armament output of the Ruhr within the limits agreed on.
North Atlantic Treaty
To anyone over 40 years old-and the principal authors of the London agreement were grown men by 1918-such optimism is incredible. The story of Germany's secret rearmament in violation of the Versailles treaty, of the complete collapse of the allied effort to halt the rebirth of German militarism, is a story not from history books, but of our own generation.
I think the situation is so critical that we should pay more attention to the suggestions which have been made by other members of this group, that the time factor is most important and Germany should have a longer time in which to demonstrate to herself and to the world that the nazi elements which were responsible for world war II are not going to be in control.
Like a number of hon. members of the house I was in Germany this summer. My wife and I had a most delightful stay. I had been there before, in 1926, and on both occasions I marvelled at the courtesies extended to people who had been their enemies such a short time before. Last summer again and again we inquired how a maniac like Hitler ever managed to get to a position in Germany where he could plunge their country and the world into war. Again and again the answer was, "But I was just a little man, there was nothing I could do." Sometimes the answer was, "If it had not been for forces outside Germany we would never have allowed him to go so far."
So I think we should give Germany a longer time to develop the democratic organizations that are being built up in that country, to demonstrate to themselves that they are capable of operating a democracy over a period of time. I should say that we did not meet any communists in Germany; there are not very many pro-communists to be found in West Germany, and I think it is fair to say that there is a very real fear of Russia. I should say something also which is not so well known, that there is a very real fear of the United States. But above all there is a very real fear of war.
Most of the people we saw did not seem to think either the United States or Russia would start a war in Germany or Europe, but they felt that some incident in Formosa or Indochina might set a spark which would plunge the world into war; and they know from vivid experience what war will mean to them.
Before I leave Germany I might mention that in the air edition of the London Times of January 17 I found the details of the proposals made in a Moscow broadcast of a week ago. Unfortunately details of these proposals

North Atlantic Treaty
were not carried by such papers as the New York Times, or at least I did not see them. Here is what Moscow proposed a week ago:
1.	Paris agreements lead to a grave complication of the whole situation in Europe.
2.	Paris agreements can bring nothing good to Germany. They will finally involve the German federal republic in the adventurous plans of preparation of a new war, which always were and always will be alien to the interests of the peoples, including the interests of the German pepole.
3.	Paris agreements will consolidate for many years the splitting of Germany and will become an obstacle to the peaceful restoration of the unity of Germany.
4.	The ratification of the Paris agreements is incompatible witth the restoration of Germany as a united peace-loving state.
5.	In the event of the ratification of the Paris agreements, the Bundestag will assume a grave responsibility for the continuation of the division of Germany as well as for the position of inferior rights in which the population of the German federal republic will be for many years.
6.	If plans for a remilitarized West Germany are abandoned free elections can be had in 1955.
7.	U.S.S.R. will come to an agreement on establishing appropriate international supervision of the holding of all-German elections.
8.	The holding of free all-German elections and the restoration of the unity of Germany would create the necessary preliminary conditions for the conclusion of a peace treaty with Germany which would finally consolidate the independence, sovereignty and equality of rights of a united Germany.
It continues:
If. however, the Paris agreements are ratified, the "U.S.S.R. would take care not only of a further strengthening of its friendly relations with the German democratic republic-
This is East Germany, of course.
-but also of facilitating the strengthening of peace and security in Europe by the joint efforts of the peace-loving European states."
I am not suggesting, Mr. Speaker, that these proposals are made with complete sincerity and that they would be accepted without qualification, but according to the London Times they have created a great deal of confusion in West Germany.
The London Times of January 20 carries a report from its Bonn correspondent outlining the views of the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, a newspaper which is usually found to be in support of the government's foreign policy. This newspaper feels that the politically undemonstrative nature of the German people conceals "a deep division disturbing the nation's subconsciousness."
The writer points out that the official western view of the statement is that it is a victory for the policy of strength, that the Russians have made concessions and will make even more if the same policy is pursued. But the danger, when the west eventually comes to negotiate with the Russians, seemed to be that the question on the agenda
TMr. Nicholson.]
will not be German reunification but the conditions for peaceful coexistence without the irritant of a united Germany. The eastern zone would then stand no chance of being freed.
I would next like to deal with the H-bomb. The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Pearkes) referred to this factor the other night. I have the greatest respect for the hon. gentleman personally and also for his very distinguished war record, but I believe the conclusion he reached is unsound. The hon. member intimated that the H-bomb probably would not be used because it was so dreadful and because both sides possessed it. I am quite sure that if the hon. member was the officer in charge the H-bomb would not be used; but unfortunately he is not.
In the U.S. News and World Report of December 31, 1954, there appeared a very alarming article by Air Marshal Sir John Slessor, former chief of the British air staff. It is headed "H-bomb Will be Used if Big War Comes." The writer claims that the weapon of mass destruction would certainly be used in any great war between major powers and he quotes Mr. Attlee, British opposition leader, as stating:
"The fact Is that once there is war, absolute war, in the modern age, and if the existence of a nation is at stake, any weapon will be used in the last resort.
The writer then goes on:
When is the last resort? It is beyond doubt that ultimately the bomb would be used-no nation would admit defeat with this terrible weapon of retaliation lying unused in its armory. Are we to wait to use it as a rat's dying bite? Are we to hold back and watch our enemy overrun Europe and set up his V-weapon sites again on the channel coast, and do nothing to stop him except with weapons of his own choosing . . .
I would like to refer hon. members to a speech by Sir Winston Churchill as reported in British Hansard of July 29. Hon. members may recall that Sir Winston was reminded by members of the Labour party of his famous statement that he did not become prime minister to preside over the liquidation of the British Empire. Mr. Attlee said that if the Prime Minister were in opposition he would describe developments in Egypt as "scuttle." Captain Waterhouse, one of the Conservative rebels, said it was not a sell-out but a give-away. Sir Winston rose to reply as follows:
I have not in the slightest degree concealed in public speech how much I regretted the course of events in Egypt. But I had not held my mind closed to the tremendous changes that have taken place in the whole strategic position in the world which make the thoughts, which were well founded and well knit together a year ago, utterly obsolete, and which have changed the opinions of every competent soldier that I have been able to meet.

Later he continued:
Merely to try to imagine in outline the first few weeks of a war under conditions about which we did not know when this session commenced, and about which we had not been told-merely to portray that picture and submit it to the house would, I am sure, convince hon. gentlemen of the obsolescence of the base and of the sense of proportion which is vitally needed at the present time, not only in military dispositions but in all our attempts to establish human relationships between nation and nation.
In the Manchester Guardian of December 21, 1954 I read the following:
"We are trying to keep an element of sanity in a nightmare world," one senior officer said.
He was speaking of allied planning for the possibility of a war with hydrogen bombs. His conclusion was that the outcome of war would probably be settled within the first 20 to 30 days, and for Britain perhaps within the first 20 or 30 hours.
In his judgment, that greatly raised the deterrent value of the American and British long-range bombing forces. . . .
There was a time when it was thought that the superiority of air power in the western countries would give us an advantage, but Joseph and Stewart Alsop, writing in the New York Herald Tribune of August 20, 1954 said:
The pentagon intelligence analysts have reluctantly concluded that the Soviet union is already producing a jet engine about twice as powerful as any yet produced in the United States. This is the biggest shock, the bitterest pill in a development that was generally shocking and unexpected. Until a few months ago, the official forecasters were convinced that the Soviet aircraft industry would need at least two years more to turn out planes comparable to our B47 and B52. But now such planes are already in the air.
To find the Soviet strategic air development two years ahead of schedule was unpleasant enough in itself. It was even more unpalatable to find that this remarkable Soviet jump forward depended upon, and in fact probably resulted from, the successful design of a jet engine greatly surpassing any jet engine as yet designed in the west.
Those who maintained that the west had superiority in aircraft and atom and hydrogen bombs have had trouble in proving their claims. The opinion I have been expressing about the inevitability of the hydrogen bomb being used has been confirmed by Viscount Montgomery. In his "Ottawa Letter" in Saturday Night of December 18, 1954, Mr. Stevenson quoted him as follows:
Speaking not long ago at the Royal United Services Institution in London. Lord Montgomery said: "I want to make it absolutely clear that we at SHAPE (the headquarters of the NATO forces) are basing all our operational planning on using atomic and thermonuclear weapons in our defence. It is no longer a question of 'they may be used'. It is very definitely 'they will be used-if we are attacked'. We could not match the strength that could be brought against us, unless we used nuclear 50433-32
North Atlantic Treaty
weapons. We have reached the point of no return, as regards the use of atomic and thermonuclear weapons in a hot war."
In another copy of The Nation I ran across an article by Elizabeth Weideman on "The H-Bomb's First Victims". An appeal was sent to the Y.W.C.A.'s all over the world by a distinguished Christian Japanese woman, Mrs. Eumura. Her letter is written in restrained language. Along with her letter is given some information with regard to the facts of the H-bomb:
In the past three years there have been reported several cases of pitiful deaths of school children who as babies survived Hiroshima or Nagasaki seemingly unharmed. These children looked quite normal until they fell ill six or seven years after that day, their bodies giving way to the destructive operation that had been secretly working within them. So far, nothing can save those in whom the symptoms of the ''atomic disease" manifest themselves, and they die after indescribable months of agony. Grown-ups are no exception to this liability . . .
Then there is a description of the sailor who lost his life as a result of the explosion of the H-bomb in Bikini. In the New York Herald of January 7 I saw a note "Japan accepts H-bomb offer", and there is a picture of-
-U.S.A. ambassador J. A. Allison shaking hands with Japanese foreign minister after Japan agreed to accept a $2 million payment from U.S.A. for damage claimed by Japan caused by an American H-bomb test at Bikini last March.
When one considers that this fishing boat was 80 miles away from where the explosion occurred, and that the United States has paid $2 million for the damage caused at that distance, it gives one some idea of the implications if we insist upon using H-bombs in a third world war. I think probably I should use the word "last" world war with "last" in quotation marks, as there will not be a fourth world war.
The last point I plan to develop is what I call an appeal to reason and I am quoting some well known people. In the Leader-Post, Regina, Saskatchewan, January 3, 1955 on the front page I read the following:
Pope Urges Coexistence on Basis of Bethlehem Dispatch from Vatican City-
Pope Pius today published a solemn appeal for the peaceful coexistence of all nations on the basis of "the principles of Bethlehem".
The appeal was contained in a Christmas message to the world, which the pontiff was too ill to complete in time for Christmas and which he was still too weak today to broadcast himself.
In apparent criticism of the recent Paris pacts the pontiff said the accords no longer looked toward extensive European unification. In the past, he had expressed approval of the European defence community.

North Atlantic Treaty
Then I go back to the speech of Sir Winston Churchill in the House of Commons in England on May 11, 1953, when he made some statements I think we should never forget. He said:
I do not believe that the immense problem of reconciling the security of Russia with the freedom and safety of western Europe is insoluble.
Then he quoted his telegram which he sent Stalin on April 29, 1945. If it was a worthwhile telegram to send in 1945, I submit that it is a worth-while sentiment to express today. Sir Winston said in his telegram:
There is not much comfort in looking into a future where you and the countries you dominate, plus the communist parties in many other states, are all drawn up on one side, and those who rally to the English-speaking nations and their associates or dominions are on the other. It is quite obvious that their quarrel would tear the world to pieces, and that all of us leading men on either side who had anything to do with that would be shamed before history. Even embarking on a long period of suspicions, of abuses and counterabuse, and of opposing policies would be a disaster hampering the great developments of world prosperity for the masses which are attainable only by our trinity. . .
Then he said:
I must make it plain that, in spite of all the uncertainties and confusion in which world affairs are plunged, I believe that a conference on the highest level should take place between the leading powers without long delay.
I might say that a well known correspondent in London informed me that Sir Winston, with a view to what the future will say of him, would prefer to be remembered as the man who saved the peace rather than in connection with the extremely important role he played during the second world war. But apparently he has not been encouraged to have a top-level conference. Then I should like to quote a well known American, George F. Kennan, former ambassador to the Soviet union. McCarthy has never suggested that Ambassador Kennan had any communist tendencies. He said:
As many of you already know, I have never seen any evidence that the Soviet leaders have at any time since world war II (or before, for that matter) desired a general war between the Soviet union and the major capitalist powers, or looked to such a war as a likely means of achieving their objectives.
I still have one other, a well known international figure, who spoke as follows:
If the nations of the world engage in a third world war, civilization would be destroyed, external affairs minister Pearson warned Sunday. . . Mr. Pearson said that "horrible devastation" would be brought about by the new atomic and chemical weapons devised by men.
"Should we ever get into world war III, there probably won't be more than a handful of people left", Mr. Pearson said.
He referred to the hydrogen bomb explosion in the Pacific and said he was glad that the public was "now becoming acquainted with the fantastic
[Mr. Nicholson.!
power of the weapon." "That one bomb in the Pacific was more devastating than all the bombs dropped on Germany and Italy during the last war."
Then he said:
"But we will never defeat communism unless we understand it. We must have faith and a positive approach. We have to confront communism with something stronger and more dynamic. . ."
"So often in the international field today, problems are not all black and white. They are often in terms of grey, and it is hard to find what is right and what is wrong."
I think the minister never uttered truer words than those, that things are not all black and white, that we cannot defeat communism unless we understand it. I suggest that if someone could devise a formula so that within the next 24 hours every communist in the world could be killed, our problems would not be solved. We really would be in trouble then, if there were no more communists left for us to attack.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I submit that the critical international situation has been created by men and women. It can be solved by men and women. I suggest that this house reject the motion which is before it and refer the question to the United Nations, an organization that we have helped to build, in the hope that this organization might be able to bring the dispute to a satisfactory conclusion.

speechtext:
shall take a very few minutes in this debate, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member who spoke before me and I entirely disagree on this matter. Because the people at home feel so strongly on the question of rearming Germany, I rise in my place for a very few moments to put their thoughts on the record.
I have given many weeks of thought to what my stand would be when the time came to vote on this question. I have argued in my mind both for rearmament and against it, hoping that out of some personal experience in this house, with years of debate in print in my office and the speeches of the Secretary of State for External Affairs to which to refer, some firm basis for an established opinion could be found.
I listened with profound respect on January 20 to the speech delivered by the minister, and I was particularly interested when he said that the democratic nations in and out of NATO seek to institute a search for effective control of thermonuclear weapons, not for warfare but for welfare. He said that agreement for effective disarmament was the goal of all those nations which comprise NATO and that for years the Canadian government had taken an active part-he could have said a leading part-in searching for such an agreement.

The minister's second point was built around the fact, acknowledged by all who welcome a permanent peace, that you can only deter aggression by strength. The improvement of relations amongst the friendly countries, the removal of the causes of war and the development of the international community, was a third area explored by the minister. Whether we forward these valiant ideas by bringing into being a rearmed Germany, though it may be under temporary control, is problematical. If we could rearm that country and guarantee to our people that this would be a permanent solution to a problem that has faced us in two wars, then we would be on sound ground in any personal action we take in voting on this motion.
Hon. members will recall that not too long ago we voted whether we should allow Kurt Meyer to return to Germany. I believe I was the only one on this side of the house who voted against his return at that time. I did it not for political advantage, not to create in the minds of the people of Canada the thought that here was a Liberal member who was against Germany, but I voted as I did because it was my opinion that concrete evidence was available that former senior nazi officials were coming to the forefront in German military matters.
If you need further evidence of that fact, press reports of Meyer's reception and consequent generous treatment in his country are proof enough. Read the headlines of the European papers and prove for yourself that the staff of any new German army will be former associates, personal or military, of the nazi regime.
It has been said many times in this debate that we can rely on Herr Adenauer to keep control of former military leaders in Germany. Perhaps he can. He is a great but elderly man, and who comes after him? Who will be there five years from now? No guarantees can be given.
I am one who believes that eventually we will fight communism in battle, communism headed by either Moscow or Peking. Indochina, Korea, Malaya, Costa Rica and Guatemala are all a pattern in an encircling movement that will force a war to the death. It may not come in my time or yours, but the Lenin formula of world domination is not too far off schedule, and certainly is not too far off course. I hold the opinion also that the war will not be an atomic war as we understand it. Complete destruction of the world could never be read into the words of Lenin.
If that war comes, or even seriously threatens, we in Canada will play a major role. There will be no choice of who will
50433-32i
North Atlantic Treaty
serve and who will stay at home. Every young Canadian, male and female, will fight that war. The fathers and mothers will fight it at home, too. There will be no static position, no trenches, no decimation of European countries and peace at home. Burnaby and Oshawa, Ottawa and Halifax, Yellowknife and Richmond, will each share in an ever-moving front line. The recent warning from General Ridgway to his President proves this possibility. He said that a reduction in the size of United States ground forces in Europe, a policy already decided upon, would cause a three-months gap in reinforcements, reinforcements to face a communist army now in being of 75 satellite divisions, over 2,500 planes, thousands of pieces of artillery both atomic and basic, and a Russian fighting force that is beyond civilian realization.
In the event of war, what would be the Canadian manpower position? As I have said, every young man and woman would be subject to immediate draft. Perhaps millions would die. Certainly Canada's casualty rate in two other wars would be fractional compared to this terrible holocaust.
I have faced up to this crisis with what I hope is mature and complete understanding. Many arguments present themselves to me and today I wish I could, in all sincerity, vote against this motion. We are voting, however, not only on what is to happen now but on what might happen to our children and Canadian generations yet unborn. I vote in support because I think there is a chance, a good chance, of delaying war for a generation. It is a far better thing that we do if we rearm a country in an effort to hold that country as our friend. If we refuse to rearm Germany, in time we create a physical enemy with only one country to which to turn, Russia. There can be no geographical neutrality in a great country surrounded by acquaintances and no military friends.
I look to the day when East Germans will join with their blood brothers in the west to bring back into being a great friend of the democracies. We perform no service to this hope by refusing to West Germany its rightful place in NATO. The defeat of this motion would mean that the western European peace alliance is dead, perhaps worse than that. I believe the defeat of the European defence community by France, and an adverse vote on this motion, would surely prove to the German people that their future does not lie with the west.
Unhappily perhaps, but with the honest opinion that I aid my country in its fight for peace, if only a temporary peace, I support this motion. The knowledge that we may face some type of aggressive Germany in

North Atlantic Treaty
the future must be outweighed by the fact we might produce a formula for world peace and understanding. This thought counterbalances any fear of the results that may come from a mistake now. If the decision of this house defends Canada against another world war in the immediate years ahead, we will have fulfilled our responsibility to those young people who attend the schools throughout Canada.

speechtext:
The previous speaker has shown, Mr. Speaker, how seriously the members of this house have taken this problem, and how deep has been their study. I am aware of the conviction with which many of them have spoken. It is possible that many of us differ. We ask that our convictions be treated as having arisen from equally great concern about the future of Canada and of the rest of the world.
Three months ago Canada's representatives signed the protocol admitting the Federal Republic of Germany into the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. It was evident even at that time that there were many serious doubts in the minds of many people, in all NATO countries, as to the wisdom of that action. It was surprising to note that the Canadian government did not consider the opinion of the people of Canada of sufficient importance to call parliament before this time to find out what the people thought and what their representatives would say with regard to the protocol.
Be that as it may, the government accepts that responsibility. But it has this advantage, that many events have taken place since the fateful October 23, 1954, which I believe have confirmed rather than diminished these doubts and misgivings. The French assembly, when called upon to ratify this agreement, rejected it on the first vote. Later they reversed their decision, but quite evidently they were under pressure. The British parliament, the cradle of democracy, adopted it with over 55 per cent of the members abstaining. It was a silent protest, but it was a protest. It was a sign that there were grave misgivings.
I think it is proof that our democracy is in a healthy condition when members register their objections, even against an overwhelming majority, and are free to express their convictions. I believe it would be wrong for this parliament to pass this ratification unanimously when it is so evident that many sincere, thoughtful and patriotic Canadians are opposed to it. And I do not include the communists in our land, who are the agents

of Russia and who would use the privileges of democracy in this land to destroy freedom here. For them I have only the deepest contempt. I will not allow them to influence my thinking.
I want to pay tribute to the leader of this group, and to other men in high ranking positions in this group, who informed the house of their honest convictions, honestly arrived at, in support of the resolution. At no time was any effort made to influence other members, nor did the other members try to influence their leader to change his mind. The vote of our group is the vote of each member, speaking from his own convictions. I am proud of our leadership, and more convinced than ever that such leadership contains within it the essence of democracy, the essence of freedom.
There is every evidence that speakers in all parts of the house have very serious doubts, and that those doubts are shared by many other people.
I intend to vote against the motion because I believe it is wrong, and that it is premature. I believe it has within it an inherent danger to the western world. I intend to vote against it because I believe it is being forced upon a reluctant people. Evidence from all parts of the country shows that the rank and file of the German people are not in favour of restoring armaments to Germany, if it is to come under nazi leadership.
If this protocol is to be successful it requires confidence. I doubt whether it will give any real strength to the western powers until it has that confidence. I believe it is possible that the implementation of this protocol may bring war closer to us, not put it farther away, because it does not contain the safeguards which I believe are necessary.
If nuclear arms of war come to this earth because man refuses to live in brotherhood, then it will be divine retribution; man can destroy himself by his own stupidity.
I want here to reaffirm my faith in the rank and file of the German people. They are capable; throughout the world they have shown themselves to be capable of great achievements, of making great contributions to the betterment of mankind. But I have only the greatest misgivings concerning them when they are dominated by a military dictatorship. We of the western world find it difficult to understand how an army could possibly superimpose its will upon the state.

But those of us who have studied German militarism and nazism know that this does happen. Those who are in power look down upon the democratic processes. They consider themselves supreme.
The rank and file of the German people fear and detest nazism. They oppose the rearmament offered them today. This is where I think the great danger comes in. I do not know whether it is part of the calculated risk about which we hear so much. Has a calculation been made of the possibility that, once that German machine is again in power with 12 divisions, once these people are rearmed under nazi leadership, it may not be possible to trust them? All Germany wants a reunited Germany. All Germany would like East Germany to be united with the west. Might not the offer be made to a nazi West Germany that Germany could be united if they would only break with the west? And if that is a possibility we should certainly study it with great care. In such event, not only would we be opposed by Russia in time of war, but also by a Russia joined with a powerful nazi machine which we ourselves had helped to recreate.
History reveals that the character of people living in certain environments produces predictable results and trends. Nazi Germany is an entirely different nation from a free and democratic Germany. The German people, brought up under a democracy, and brought into an economic alliance with the western world, which has learned the meaning of true democracy, could be a great ally. But we do not know what a nazi Germany would do. No one knows what they would do. Give Germany democracy, real co-operation and time to build a true Germany, time to cleanse itself of nazism, and we will have hope. Some day in the not too distant future this could be achieved. At that time a rearming of Germany could be tried with some hope of success.
Had article 2 of NATO been properly implemented we might have had such a Germany today. The people of that country would have had a chance to throw out nazism. The teachings of Hitler remain too deeply rooted for us to hope that this change could be brought about in such a short time. If there were evidence to show that nazism had gone, then there might be some justification for taking a calculated risk. But instead of evidence that nazism is gone, what do we find? We find Kurt Meyer welcomed home. We find Adolf Galland, chief inspector of the luftwaffe fighting command, returning to
North Atlantic Treaty
Germany from Argentina. We have Frau Schlitter making a statement in London showing the tragic reality that the nazi thinking is not dead. Hitler's militarism can never be accepted in faith by the western world. That record can never be forgotten. That black page in the history of man is written.
We have not done our part to help build the real Germany, the democratic Germany. Canada must take her blame along with the rest. We must reap today the harvest of that failure. There is to be a new 500,000-man army under Adenauer, with its generals pledged to NATO. That is a fait accompli. The pact has been signed. The evidence that the majority here are with it is complete. We can only hope that there may be some force live enough and great enough to hold it within control.
The trouble is with that army of half a million men there may be a few staff members under Adenauer who are denazified and who believe in NATO, but who is going to officer that army, who are the staffs going to be, from the lieutenant colonels and colonels down to the majors, the non-commissioned officers and the ranks? Who is to be enlisted from the ranks of the German people? Therein lies the greatest danger in our control over Germany today. Reports confirm one or two things. One, that there is a great hope amongst all the German people that ultimate unification will take place and they will be united with their brothers in East Germany.
The other great thing is the great mistrust of the rank and file of the German people of nazi regimentation. I refuse to support a nazi German army forced upon a reluctant German people who know the real nazis. Give them time. Give the world time to appreciate the consequences of refusing to live together, to realize that war has never settled anything, that mass destruction can be the punishment for refusing to live in human brotherhood.

You cannot condemn a whole organization if a part of it goes astray. You do not shoot a man just because he has gangrene in his leg, but there is occasion to cut the leg off if the whole body is to be saved. I think, though, this is a very good thing for Canada. Certainly, because of the speeches we have heard from that group and by the vote that will be taken we shall be able to separate the sheep from the goats, and possibly with the goats we shall have to put those who fail to vote; because I heard one remarkable speech from that side indicating that everybody should vote against the rearming of Germany. After a 30-minute speech the hon. member sat down, but before he did so he said he was not going to vote along the lines he suggested, and in fact he was not going to vote at all. The only thing that told me was that he did not have the courage of his convictions. It was a proposition of do as I say, but not as I do.
From time to time many words have come out from Moscow. We have had those echoed by the C.C.F. members of the legislature in Saskatchewan, who have always supported the ideas that have come from that country but without taking the alternative in any case. These things make one wonder.
In this debate these gentlemen who have indicated that they are not going to support their leader have taken one side of the story only. I have not heard any part of the other side. They have not discussed the alternative.

COMMONS	'	*
I have no objection to a man looking at both sides. He comes to his honest opinion; he decides which is which, and that is all right. But these gentlemen have discussed the terrible things that might happen if we allow those 12 divisions to be established in Germany. Well, they might have mentioned the other 250 divisions that are in existence in Russia and her satellites. In East Germany we have 180,000 so-called police, equipped with some 600 tanks, 250 mobile guns and 1,700 pieces of artillery. Well, that is some police force.
As the minister told us, there was no rearming whatsoever in Western Germany in 1948. There was not even a soldier there. But that was when the rearming of East Germany took place. In view of our experience with Germany, you might think there is cause for serious thought. The minister has told us of the safeguards we have there. But with the 250 divisions and this East German police force and another 400,000 Soviet troops in that country, what are the safeguards in that case? Do we hear anything about those? Not at all.
Then, Mr. Speaker, we have had calls on members of this house. I have had telephone calls from some of these people, and I told them they had access to my office, that I was quite willing to see them and hear what they had to say. One delegation was supposed to meet me in the morning, but they failed to arrive. They telephoned me in the afternoon and said they were sorry, that there was some misunderstanding and they could not see me. But I did have a one-man delegation call on me. He was a gentleman from my own riding. This gentleman had been the communist candidate in the last election. He is quite forthright about what he wants; he always has been. I have no disagreement with that. What he wants here is a Soviet government. He is quite willing for Russia to come here and take over.
We have no communist members as such in this house, but when one reads the speeches that we have heard from some hon. members of the group across the way who are showing signs of dissent with their leader, it indicates that there has at least been some acquiescence in what has been proposed by the Soviet union, and that the voice of Moscow has not been unheard in this house.
